items.title: 36th TAS Mobile Training Team conducts Airfield Operations Training with Indonesian Air Force
items.author: SrA Manasseh Demissie
items.summary: U.S. Airmen with the 36th Tactical Advisory Squadron trained Indonesian Air Force personnel during a Mobile Training Team engagement in Jakarta, Indonesia, Aug. 24-28, 2026.
items.body:
JAKARTA, Indonesia – U.S. Airmen with the 36th Tactical Advisory Squadron trained Indonesian Air Force personnel during a Mobile Training Team engagement in Jakarta, Indonesia, Aug. 24-28, 2026.

The bilateral training focused on aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicle operations, as well as maintenance and emergency airfield lighting systems. The engagement marked the second iteration of this type of training in Indonesia.

“This engagement was one step toward helping our partners meet their airfield operations objectives under the building partnership capacity mission,” said U.S. Air Force Staff Sgt. Cole Tomin, a 36th TAS air adviser.

The defense cooperation framework between the U.S. and Indonesia is centered around the Major Defense Cooperation Partnership, which outlines key mission sets, including exercises and operational partnerships.

“Mobile training team missions allow the 36th Tactical Advisory Squadron to work directly with partner nations and provide training based on their operational needs,” said U.S. Air Force Tech. Sgt. Richard Bazell, 36th TAS advanced air adviser and team lead. “These engagements help us build relationships, understand partner requirements and support their efforts to develop capabilities for future operations.”

The 36th TAS acquired subject matter experts from across the 36th Wing, including a fire protection craftsman, vehicle maintenance mechanic and an electrical contingency instructor.

Their efforts focused on firetruck maintenance, operations and emergency airfield lighting systems to enhance the Indonesian Air Force’s ability to respond to airfield emergencies.

Air Force instructors noted the training enhances their capability to work alongside Indonesia.

“The goal was to give the Indonesian Air Force personnel practical instructions on how emergency airfield lighting equipment is set up and used to support airfield operations,” said U.S. Air Force Tech. Sgt. Jason Taylor, an electrical contingency instructor with the 554th Rapid Engineer Deployable Heavy Operational Repair Squadron Engineers.

The lighting system provides reliable visual guidance and illumination for aircraft operations when primary airfield lighting or power sources are unavailable.

“I came here specifically to help train on the aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicle,” said U.S. Air Force Staff Sgt. David Delafunte, a fire truck and refueling maintenance craftsmen assigned to the 36th Logistics Readiness Squadron. “I helped the Indonesian firefighters with component identification, troubleshooting and overall maintenance of the aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicle.”

The ARFF vehicle training enables rapid respond to airfield emergencies, high-intensity fuel and aircraft fires, and joint support between U.S. and Indonesia to protect military assets.

This type of engagement supports the 36th TAS mission to advise, assist and support partners across the Indo-Pacific through airfield operation instructions and technical exchanges.

“For the future we plan to continue to provide EALS training, covering maintenance and engineers’ assistant guidance on where to place the equipment,” Bazell said. “We hope through these engagements we can strengthen their airfield operations and our partnership.” -30-

items.title: From Annapolis to the Front Lines of Sovereignty: How a U.S. Naval Academy Graduate Helps Defend the West Philippine Sea
items.author: LT Drew Verbis
items.summary: The waters of the West Philippine Sea have become one of the world's most consequential maritime flashpoints. Competing territorial claims, increasingly assertive actions by the People's Republic of China, and the growing importance of a free and open Indo-Pacific have transformed the region into a defining test of international law, deterrence and national sovereignty.
items.body:
The waters of the West Philippine Sea have become one of the world's most consequential maritime flashpoints. Competing territorial claims, increasingly assertive actions by the People's Republic of China, and the growing importance of a free and open Indo-Pacific have transformed the region into a defining test of international law, deterrence and national sovereignty.

Standing at the center of that challenge is Philippine Navy Rear Adm. Vincent J. Sibala, Commander of Naval Command West—a U.S. Naval Academy graduate whose journey from Annapolis to Palawan reflects the enduring purpose of military education: preparing leaders to confront the strategic challenges of their generation.

For Sibala, command extends far beyond directing ships or conducting naval operations. Every mission, he said, must ultimately connect to something larger: protecting the Filipino people and defending the sovereignty of the nation.

“You have to understand the entire mission,” Sibala said. “Our responsibility ultimately comes back to protecting our people, securing the sovereignty of the state and preserving the integrity of our national territory. If you only think about conducting naval operations, you are missing the larger purpose of why we are here.”

It is a philosophy that connects tactical action to strategic purpose—every patrol, every watch and every Sailor contributing to the defense of the Philippine nation.

That responsibility has grown increasingly urgent.

Repeated encounters between Philippine and Chinese forces, coercive activities at sea and concerns surrounding Chinese rocket launches have underscored the changing regional security environment. Sibala views those events not simply as isolated incidents, but as part of a broader pattern requiring sustained attention.

“Essentially, they are firing across our bow—repeatedly,” Sibala said. “The danger is allowing that behavior to become normal. We have to recognize what is happening, prepare for it and communicate the urgency before a crisis forces us to react.”

That concern reflects a broader lesson Sibala emphasizes when discussing the West Philippine Sea: strategic challenges become more difficult when repeated behavior is gradually accepted as routine.

“Sometimes the problem is not only the source of the challenge,” he said. “It is our failure to address it. It becomes normalized. We begin to accept it—and then we panic when things finally blow up.”

For Sibala, understanding that pattern requires more than watching what happens today. It requires thinking deeply about history, strategy and the decisions available to commanders before a crisis arrives. That intellectual approach was sharpened thousands of miles away in Annapolis.

Sibala credits much of his strategic outlook to the U.S. Naval Academy, where he learned that developing officers requires far more than mastering procedures or memorizing history. The Academy challenged future leaders to question assumptions, understand context and consider decisions for which there may be no predetermined answer.

He remembers one classroom question in particular. Rather than asking students simply to describe what happened during a historical naval battle, an instructor placed them in the commander's position and asked what they would have done.

The lesson stayed with him.

“It forces you to understand that knowing what happened is not enough,” Sibala said. “You have to understand why it happened—the conditions, the logistics, the information available to the commander. Your understanding has to go deeper.”

He also remembers guidance from then-U.S. Naval Academy Superintendent Vice Adm. Virgil Hill about the purpose of developing midshipmen.

“The purpose was not to train good midshipmen,” Sibala recalled. “It was to prepare good officers. As a leader, that is your responsibility—prepare people for the job they will eventually have to do.”

Combined with lessons from the Philippine Military Academy—including Max Ehrmann's Desiderata and the poem Don't Quit—those experiences helped shape a philosophy rooted in resilience, humility and disciplined judgment.

They also reinforced something Sibala understood from the beginning: his education abroad carried an obligation to return home and improve the institution he would serve.

“I knew I was training with the best,” Sibala said. “But I also knew I had a responsibility to bring what you learned back and help raise the standard of the service.”

Today, that responsibility reaches directly into the West Philippine Sea.

Sibala argues that one of the Philippine military's most important transformations has not been a particular ship, weapon or sensor, but a change in how it understands the security environment.

After decades focused heavily on internal security, he came to believe the Armed Forces of the Philippines needed to look increasingly outward.

“I realized the existential threat was outside, not inside,” Sibala said. “We had to change the mindset—to understand that we cannot remain focused only on ourselves when the larger challenge affects not just the Philippines, but the entire region.”

That changing environment also requires military leaders to think differently about the future of warfare. Unmanned systems, cyber operations, electronic warfare and long-range precision capabilities are rapidly redefining the character of conflict. Preparing for tomorrow, Sibala argues, means resisting the institutional temptation to perfect the methods of yesterday.

“The nature of war stays the same, but its character evolves with technology,” he said. “We cannot prepare for the future by becoming experts in the last war.”

He illustrated that point with characteristic humor while recalling his observations following an amphibious landing during Exercise Balikatan.

After watching the exercise, Sibala was asked to provide his assessment.

“I told them, ‘I am happy to report that we are now ready for World War III.’”

The room laughed.

The implication was considerably more serious.

“It was good that we learned from previous wars,” Sibala said. “But we are preparing for the future. We cannot remain stuck with what we learned from the last war.”

That future is also increasingly multinational.

As the U.S.-Philippine alliance continues to evolve, Sibala views cooperation not as a requirement that two nations agree on every issue, but as the product of understanding where their interests and values align.

Sibala states this alignment is increasingly visible through Task Force Philippines (TF-P), which works alongside the AFP to coordinate U.S. military support to the Philippine-led Comprehensive Archipelagic Defense Concept; representing a contemporary expression of the alliance Sibala first experienced personally as a Filipino midshipman in Annapolis.

For Sibala, however, the strength of an alliance begins before ships sail together or forces enter an exercise area.

“Understand your interests. Understand the other nation’s interests. Then look at where they overlap,” Sibala said. “If there is commonality in your values and interests, that is where you start.”

For younger Sailors and officers, bilateral and multilateral exercises provide something equally important: exposure to different ways of thinking. They allow service members to see how allies and partners approach problems, make decisions and operate under pressure.

Sibala knows the value of that exposure personally.

He was once the young Filipino officer sent across the Pacific to learn from another navy.

Today, he makes a point of reaching out to Philippine midshipmen attending American service academies because he remembers how uncommon such mentorship was during his own years in Annapolis.

“That is part of my responsibility,” Sibala said. “You bring these young people up the right way, give them direction and prepare them for the challenges they are going to face when they come back.”

And they will return to a security environment considerably different from the one Sibala entered decades ago.

Asked what advice he would offer those future officers, however, Sibala did not turn to theories of deterrence, emerging technology or great-power competition.

Instead, he returned to one of the simplest lessons he had ever received.

Years ago, former Philippine Navy Flag Officer Vice Adm. Victorino Hingco delivered a message that initially struck the young Sibala as almost disappointingly brief: “ Know your job and do it well.”

At the time, Sibala wondered how such a simple sentence could possibly capture everything expected of an officer.

Decades of command changed his perspective.

“I remember it to this day,” Sibala said. “It is very simple, but it is very true. Sometimes the simpler the message, the more it resonates.”

More than three decades after Sibala left the Philippines for Annapolis, those words have followed him to one of the Indo-Pacific's most strategically significant maritime frontiers.

The young midshipman who once waited months to exchange letters with home now commands Philippine Sailors operating in waters where decisions can carry consequences far beyond Palawan. Technology has changed. The strategic environment has changed. The character of warfare continues to change.

The fundamental obligation of an officer has not.

For Sibala, the path from Annapolis to the West Philippine Sea ultimately returns to the same principle the Academy sought to instill decades ago: prepare officers not simply for the challenges they face today, but for the responsibilities their nation will ask them to carry tomorrow.

And when that responsibility arrives: Know your job. Do it well.

items.title: Strengthening Connections: Okinawan Catholic High School students visit MCAS Futenma
items.author: 1LT Byshup Rhodes
items.summary: Military actions can feel obscure. People outside of the military are often unaware of what it’s like within the gates of the base. That lack of awareness increases when not only is there a separation between military and civilian, but also a separation between American and Japanese culture. The relationship between Japan and America is essential to the stability of the Pacific region. Underneath that broader relationship is the connection between the people on the ground living the relationship
items.body:
CAMP FOSTER, Okinawa—Military actions can feel obscure. People outside of the military are often unaware of what it’s like within the gates of the base. That lack of awareness increases when not only is there a separation between military and civilian, but also a separation between American and Japanese culture.

The relationship between Japan and America is essential to the stability of the Pacific region. Underneath that broader relationship is the connection between the people on the ground living the relationship daily—the American service members and the locals of the Japanese host nation.

To foster this vital relationship, and to clarify the often-murky waters of military operations, students from Okinawa Catholic High School were invited to visit Marine Corps Air Station (MCAS) Futenma.

Led by Major Nicholas Rhea, installation operations officer at MCAS Futenma, the visit took the students on a tour through the MCAS Futenma headquarters building, the air traffic control tower, a hangar and inside aircraft.

Rhea explained the purpose of the visit was to remove the mystery of what happens within the gates of the base, as well as to strengthen the connection between the military and the Okinawan locals.

“We aimed to demystify what happens behind the gates of MCAS Futenma,” said Rhea.“It was about showing these young citizens that we aren't just a military installation; we are their neighbors, committed to safety, partnership and mutual respect.”

The first location on the tour was the headquarters building where the students received a presentation of MCAS Futenma’s history and its units (and their aircraft). This gave the students a sense of the shared history and long-standing connection between Marines and Okinawans.

During the question-and-answer portion of the presentation, the students had the chance to speak with Rhea about his responsibilities as a leader, and with MCAS Futenma MLAs (master labor agreement) personnel about topics such as operating the chow hall and becoming a base employee.

In his responses, Rhea highlighted how operations completed at MCAS Futenma serve not only to enhance combined military readiness, but also to strengthen community partnerships.

“Our efforts here at MCAS Futenma, ”started Rhea, “are centered around not only ensuring that we are able to respond to any-and-all challenges within this area of operations, but also that we continue to maximize our mutually beneficial relationship with our Japanese allies.”

After Rhea’s comments, the MLAs shared their roles within base operations. The students were interested in the ways MLAs contributed to base success.

MLAs serve as shining representations of the continued collaboration between the US and Japan, as they symbolize the integration of local customs, beliefs and understanding into base operations.

In an interview, the chief of Local National Programs with Marine Corps Installation Pacific, Junko Taira stated, “the MLA is a labor agreement between the US and Japanese governments, based on the US-Japan Status of Forces Agreement, designed to support the US military.” MLAs have been supporting a part of the US and Japanese mission since 1957.

After the presentation, the group moved to the air traffic control tower to speak with Marines about their jobs and to get a unique view of the flightline. The Marines explained the complexities of their daily roles and shared fun anecdotes with the students.

“Fortunately, I’ve never had to deal with a crash,” said one of the Marines in the tower as he shared a laugh with the student that asked if he had he ever witnessed a crash.

The final stop on the tour was one of the hangars where students got to ask pilots questions and see aircraft firsthand.

Capt. Matthew Diddle, a CH-53E pilot assigned to Marine Heavy Helicopter Squadron 361said thathe had a good experience speaking with the students.

“I genuinely enjoyed taking time to show students the CH-53E up close and share something I’m passionate about,” said Diddle. “Letting them see the aircraft and sit in the cockpit was a great opportunity to leave a lasting, positive impression on the students.”

Capt. David Gray, a UH-1Y pilot with Marine Light Attack Helicopter Squadron (HMLA) 367, echoed the sentiment of leaving a positive impression on the students. He shared how exciting it was to have the chance to speak with such enthusiastic students.

“With us regularly flying overhead, it’s important to engage with, and to leave a positive impression on, the young people growing up in the community surrounding the base, ”said Gray. “It was also cool to be reminded that high schoolers are pretty much the same no matter the culture.”

The students smiled as they examined the aircraft. They had many questions they wanted to ask the pilots as the tour ended. Had it not been for the tour ending, the students and pilots would still be on the flightline exchanging questions and answers.

The sustained partnership between the US and Japan is essential to effective operation within the Pacific region. Continued collaboration maintains an alliance built to overcome challenges together.

Events like the student visit are an opportunity to deepen the connection between the US and Japan and strengthen their pivotal alliance. Capt. Nathaniel Thorne, an AH-1Z pilot, with HMLA-367 clarified the importance of the student visit: “it was an incredible opportunity to give back to a community that has done so much for us.” The shared experience between each side of the alliance ensures the continued success within the region.

items.title: F-16 Crashes During Training Exercise in Michigan; Pilot Ejects
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: An F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the Texas Air National Guard’s 149th Fighter Wing crashed during a training mission in Michigan on Sept. 17. The fighter's sole pilot ejected and is in stable condition at a local hospital. The post F-16 Crashes During Training Exercise in Michigan; Pilot Ejects appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

An F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the Texas Air National Guard’s 149th Fighter Wing crashed during a training mission in Michigan on Sept. 17.

The fighter’s sole pilot ejected safely. The Michigan State Police said in a social media post the pilot is in stable condition at a local hospital and there are no other known injuries related to the crash.

In a statement, the wing said the aircraft was conducting a “routine training mission” in the afternoon at Alpena Combat Readiness Training Center, a Michigan Air National Guard facility in the northern part of the state near Traverse City. The F-16 is based at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas.

The 149th is participating in an exercise called “Operation Northern Cactus” as part of training for deployment to an “austere environment,” according to information the wing released earlier this week.

The wing said the crash is under investigation.

The stricken F-16’s wingman told air traffic control that the crashed aircraft may have suffered a bird strike and said the pilot planned to bail out of the fighter before ultimately ejecting, according to audio recorded by the website LiveATC. The audio indicates the two planes were flying together on the mission as call sign BUCK 11 flight.

Imagery posted to social media showed a large plume of black smoke rising from the area. Buildings within a one-mile radius of the crash were evacuated due to a “hazardous chemical spill,” according to the State Police. F-16s carry hydrazine, a highly toxic chemical that fuels the plane’s emergency power unit, which powers the jet’s flight controls and other critical systems in the event of an engine failure.

Sept. 17, 2026

The Air Force’s new Collaborative Combat Aircraft will take part in their first large-force engagement exercise in December, the head of the drones’ Experimental Operations Unit said Sept. 15.

The Pentagon announced a deal with Lockheed Martin on Sept. 17 to expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, an advanced new Air Force and Navy air-to-air missile meant to equip fifth- and sixth-generation fighters.

Sept. 16, 2026

Lockheed Martin has unveiled its concept for a modular version of one of the Air Force’s main air-to-ground cruise missiles, opening up a range of possible upgrades and uses for the weapon.

The new head of Air Mobility Command said Sept. 16 he wants to explore an unmanned option for the service’s next-generation aerial refueling system.

The Air Force will consider acquiring new F-16 Fighting Falcon jets to answer capacity shortfalls in its aging fighter fleet, according to multiple people familiar with the matter. items.title: Former AFSOC command chief found guilty, sentenced
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: U.S. Air Force Chief Master Sgt. Anthony Green, former command chief of Air Force Special Operations Command, was found guilty of committing four offenses in violation of two articles of the Uniform Code of Military Justice to include indecent recording in violation of Article 120c; and possessing, viewing and producing child pornography in violation of Article 134 today.
items.body:
HURLBURT FIELD, Fla. – U.S. Air Force Chief Master Sgt. Anthony Green, former command chief of Air Force Special Operations Command, was found guilty of committing four offenses in violation of two articles of the Uniform Code of Military Justice to include indecent recording in violation of Article 120c; and possessing, viewing and producing child pornography in violation of Article 134 today.

He was sentenced to a reduction in rank to the grade of E-1; a dishonorable discharge; 10 years of confinement for producing child pornography; and two years of confinement each for the offenses of indecent recording, possessing child pornography, and viewing child pornography. Those sentences will run concurrently. The sentencing followed a general court-martial trial by a judge at Hurlburt Field, Florida, Sept. 14 – 17, 2026.

The offenses were committed on or near Hurlburt Field, against one victim. The Department of the Air Force Office of Special Trial Counsel preferred and referred these charges to a general court-martial and served as lead counsel for the United States during trial.

Green was acquitted of obstructing justice.

AFSOC is committed to the welfare of our Airmen and maintaining good order and discipline to preserve the trust placed in us to execute our critical global missions.

items.title: Blueprint to Better: Innovation in Action
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: Danielle Meaux Burks placed third in the Blueprint to Better competition for her idea "Responsible AI for Smarter Construction Delivery."
items.body:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. – When the Blueprint to Better competition was announced in May , Sacramento District employees were encouraged to propose ideas in which the district can improve operations in terms of efficiency and AI use. For one employee, this was an opportunity to present an innovative idea that she already implements in her work.

Engineering Technician and Office Engineer Danielle Meaux Burks submitted her idea “Responsible AI for Smarter Construction Delivery” and placed third in the competition.

Having a crucial role in construction delivery, Meaux Burks spends a lot of her time reading through proposals and construction modifications that can be worth anywhere from $20,000 to millions of dollars.

It is Meaux Burks’ job to provide the cost analysis for these proposals and draft the Price Objective Memorandum (POM) and Price Negotiation Memorandum (PNM) – a job that requires great attention to detail as proposals can be upward of thousands of pages long. Sorting through these pages could take days to complete.

“I started realizing how much of my time was being spent just finding, sorting, and organizing information before I could even get to the part that really requires my experience and judgment,” Meaux Burks said.

That changed in 2025, when the Department of War approved GenAI.mil for use with certain Controlled Unclassified Information, allowing Meaux Burks to use the platform to support aspects of her work that previously required extensive manual review.

“It was like a world of difference,” Meaux Burks said as she could now upload lengthy proposals to GenAI.mil and request information such as:

Analyze the cost that the contractor is proposing and compare it to the work we are asking them to do

Analyze the labor costs

Analyze the crew size

Now, instead of manually sorting through information on her own, Meaux Burks had a research assistant. Within minutes, she could organize project correspondence, create timelines of events, and analyze cost information. However, Meaux Burks still validates all information provided by AI through extensive review and ensuring she understands the contract and the project. She is also responsible for documenting the process properly to present decisions to district leadership.

“I'm still making the decisions,” Meaux Burks said. “I'm using AI to assist me with the research and the paperwork.”

As Meaux Burks gained experience in these platforms, she ultimately gained the confidence to submit this as an idea to the Blueprint to Better competition.

“My idea is really pretty simple: use approved AI tools to help with the repetitive, information-heavy parts of our work while keeping people responsible for the actual analysis and decisions,” she said.

When implemented in the construction delivery process, using AI could lead to faster modifications and more efficient delivery, improved cost analysis, better documentation, faster information retrieval, and so on.

For example, on one recent project, Meaux Burks used AI to assist with reviewing and organizing a contractor proposal that was hundreds of pages long and with developing a detailed timeline of events from multiple project documents spanning approximately two years.

“I estimate AI reduced the time spent on initial document review, information extraction, organization, and timeline development by approximately 70% to 80%, reducing what could have taken several days of manual effort to a matter of hours,” she said. “It also saved approximately 1 to 2 days in developing the associated POM and PNM.”

The Blueprint to Better competition required all participants to present their ideas to the Executive Leadership Council. During her presentation, Meaux Burks was able to use examples like the one previously mentioned where using approved AI tools led to better construction delivery.

“I think sometimes we assume an innovation has to be something completely new or complicated,” Meaux Burks said. “It doesn't. If you've found a better way to do something, or you keep thinking, ‘Why are we still doing it this way?’ there's probably something worth exploring.”

items.title: USSF Leaders Lay Out the Path to More Than Double the Force
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: When Space Force leaders started talking about expanding the service early this year, the idea was simple: double the size of the force in the next five years. At AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week, officials detailed just how they’re planning to grow so much so quickly. The post USSF Leaders Lay Out the Path to More Than Double the Force appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —When Space Force leaders started talking about expanding the service early this year, the idea was simple: double the size of the force in the next five years.

At AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week, officials detailed just how they’re planning to grow so much so quickly—and it goes beyond doubling.

As things stand, the Space Force has less than 11,000 uniformed Guardians and around 5,000 civilian employees . Senior leaders said at AFA their goal is to reach 25,000 uniformed and 12,500 civilian Guardians—a combined increase of about 134 percent. A service spokesperson confirmed the plan is to reach those numbers by fiscal 2031.

Brig. Gen. Christopher Fernengel, former director of plans and programs on the Space Staff, had laid out those numbers earlier this year , but talk of doubling the force led many to assume the service was aiming for 20,000 uniformed Guardians by 2030.

Lt. Gen. David N. Miller Jr., the service’s top planner, reaffirmed the higher numbers during a panel discussion at the conference—and suggested those still might not be high enough.

“As much as I know we need 25,000 Guardians in the next five years, as much as I know we need about 12,500 civilians in the Space Force in the next five years, the actual requirement, I could argue, is more,” said Miller, who serves as deputy chief of space operations for strategy, plans, programs, and requirements.

The Need

The need for more people, USSF leaders say, is driven in part by new missions. The Space Force is preparing to launch scores of new satellites to track both air and ground targets and investing in what it calls “ space control ”—the ability to protect assets in space and hold adversaries’ space assets at risk. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink even made global headlines when he revealed for the first time at the conference that the Space Force has on-orbit space control weapons.

New missions requires more personnel to execute them, especially because the Space Force isn’t backing off any of its existing efforts, said Chief Master Sergeant of the Space Force John F. Bentivegna.

“Doubling the size just makes sense given all the things we have to do,” Bentivegna said. “Even though we’re killing it today with just under 11,000 Guardians, we need more.”

Indeed, Lt. Gen. Gregory Gagnon noted that the growth in the workforce is actually smaller than the growth in equipment and systems the Space Force is poised to see.

“We are already controlling 33 to 50 percent more satellites in outer space today than two years ago,” Gagnon, the head of Combat Forces Command, said. “In the next three years, with our budget funding, we will command and control over 500 percent more. That’s a fivefold increase in the amount of kit that will be in outer space, and the people to do that will be the Guardians that we need to double in mass.”

Gagnon said his command, which presents forces to combatant commanders around the globe, is already seeing “exponentially” more demand for space capabilities.

“Of the six geographic combatant commands, all of them are asking me for help,” he said. To meet that demand, he added, two-thirds of the Space Force’s planned growth will go toward generating “more combat crews and more force elements” for commanders.

Adding People

In discussions about growing the Space Force, officials have no concern about attracting enough people—after all, the service has easily met its recruiting goals every year of its existence and has even had to turn away thousands of interested recruits and transfers. The service has so much interest, Bentivegna and others have taken to saying the Space Force doesn’t recruit new members—it “scouts” them.

In order to meet its growth goals in a “sustainable” way, the service needs to be strategic, said Deputy Chief of Space Operations for personnel Katharine Kelley.

“It is arguably easier to just say, ‘I need this many new Guardians,’” said Kelley. “It is much harder to say, ‘I need to seed all of that talent inside the service that already exists and not create an imbalance in an up-or-out promotion system.’”

Too many new Guardians with little experience entering at the lowest ranks could wreak havoc on the service’s grade structure, she noted.

“We’re trying to balance not having all of our accessions be brand new in terms of experience,” she said. “We’re looking for ways to make sure that we can kind of balance this as a sourcing model and a sustainment model for people.”

One way is direct commissioning, allowing civilians with relevant space experience to join the service at a higher rank and grade, Kelley said. Another way is interservice transfers—the Space Force just opened its application window for such transfers from the Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps in fiscal 2027.

Inevitably, though, the makeup of the force will likely change, said Bentivegna—the Space Force has always been unique among the services given its high proportion of officers to enlisted, and while it’s unlikely to approach the ratio of the Air Force or Marine Corps, the coming growth is expected to favor the enlisted side.

“We’re going to grow more enlisted than we are going to grow officer,” Bentivegna said. “I think just a couple years ago it was almost a flat 50/50. Now we’re 53 percent enlisted, and I think that will continue to grow.”

The Pipeline

No matter what, every new Guardian that the Space Force accepts will have to go through training of some sort. That means a huge influx for Space Training and Readiness Command.

In 2027 alone, STARCOM boss Maj. Gen. James E. Smith said, his command will have to train up:

Three times as many total Guardians as 2026: 1,000 to 3,000

Twice as many enlisted: 700 to 1,400

Four times as many officers: 400 to 1,600

Smith called that growth “a huge, huge scaling problem.” In response, STARCOM has raced to add around 75 new instructors at its various schools and courses.

The Space Force has always relied on the Air Force for support functions, and it will do so even more with the increased training workload, Smith said. But at the same time, the service has to continue to carve out its own identity of “Guardianship” and ensure the training is Space Force-centric.

“It’s not just enough to create a pipeline to create more Guardians,” Smith said. “We’ve got to have Guardians have the right skill sets to execute these new missions.”

Part of that, Smith said, is continuing an effort that was a top priority under former Chief of Space Operations Gen. B. Chance Saltzman: improving the service’s test and training equipment .

“There are some pieces still missing in our recipe. One of them is a fully constructed live, virtual, and constructive environment in order to do both tests, but also to do training,” Smith said.

This March, the Space Force issued a request for proposals for a physical test and training range that will feature a mix of ground and space-based systems. Officials have said they are looking to identify near-term gaps in test and training ranges and quickly field capabilities to address them.

Infrastructure

Test and training ranges are just some of the infrastructure needs the Space Force must address with its coming expansion.

Kathryn Kolbe, assistant deputy chief of space operations for installations and logistics, said the service still faces “significant infrastructure shortfalls” and is trying to address them through expanded military construction.

“For the [fiscal 2027] budget, we submitted the largest investment in MILCON in Space Force history,” Kolbe said. “If appropriated, we would receive $2.2 billion.”

Almost half of that, $1 billion, would go toward building four new space operations centers . The service is also seeking an undisclosed classified total for five new tactical electronic warfare centers. And leaders have been investing billions of dollars in infrastructure to support more launches at its ranges on Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Fla., and Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif.

All this construction will take time, though, and the personnel growth is coming fast.

“In the meantime, we’re building temporary facilities for our operational units, for our training units, and for other requirements as they arise, as we plan, program, design, and construct our long-term facilities and infrastructure,” Kolbe said.

items.title: CCA Drones to Fly at Large-Scale Air Force Exercise in December
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: The Air Force’s new Collaborative Combat Aircraft will take part in their first large-force engagement exercise in December, the head of the drones’ Experimental Operations Unit said Sept. 15. The post CCA Drones to Fly at Large-Scale Air Force Exercise in December appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —The Air Force’s new Collaborative Combat Aircraft will take part in their first large-force engagement exercise in December, the head of the drones’ Experimental Operations Unit said Sept. 15.

The Emerald Flag exercise, which will take place at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida, will be CCAs’ “first dip of the toe in an actual force integration,” Lt. Col. Lyndon Bartlett, commander of the unit, said in a panel at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.

Flying CCAs alongside manned fighters will help build the foundations necessary to one day use them in real-world operations, Bartlett said.

“That will, in [my] mind, be the first time that we will ever do some CCA end-to-end kill chain live,” Bartlett said. “That’s the first time we’ll ever be integrated in a fourth- and fifth-gen combined [offensive counter-air] push. It’ll be small, but those type of building blocks are where, I think, you get the intangibles like trust in the CCA.”

CCAs are semi-autonomous fighter drones that will, in some cases, fly alongside crewed fighters such as the F-35 or the upcoming F-47, and be directed by those fighters’ pilots using a tablet interface. The Air Force wants to have at least 500 CCAs by 2032, and plans a total fleet of 1,000 or more. So far, the service has committed to buying two CCAs—General Atomics’ FQ-42A Vengeance and Anduril Industries’ FQ-44A Fury—but more are planned.

Since the EOU was stood up at Creech Air Force Base, Nev., in June 2025, it has flown and experimented with CCAs to figure out how Airmen can best use them in combat.

During that time, Bartlett said, the EOU has been “pleasantly surprised” to learn how easy CCAs are to maintain and how small of a footprint they require to operate and sustain.

In a series of recent Agile Combat Employment exercises , he said, “we’re at a one-to-one maintainer-to-airplane ratio, which is crazy small.”

That simplicity will make it easier to have “cross-functional” Airmen take on work generating CCA sorties, even if those duties aren’t in their normal career fields, Bartlett said.

“Because [CCAs are] a little bit simpler, because their role is so focused, what we found … any [Air Force Specialty Code] can be trained to generate sorties, to load weapons,” Bartlett said. “We’ve done some of those things already, and we’re going to do a lot more experimentation over the next couple of years.”

Col. Timothy Helfrich, the portfolio acquisition executive for fighters and advanced aircraft, also said at the panel that the EOU is flying CCA aircraft “multiple times a week.”

Jason Levin, Anduril’s senior vice president of engineering, said the company delivered its FQ-44 Fury drone to the EOU in August. And in recent months, the process for operating Fury has been streamlined to the point where “it’s down to a single operator flying a Fury from a laptop,” Levin said.

“They were doing disaggregated operations, flying from multiple locations,” Levin said. “They were doing hot reloads on Fury, so getting it down from hours down to single-digit minutes to turn the jet. They’re really pushing the envelope, flying with mission autonomy. It was the first time Air Force operators were flying with mission autonomy on Fury multiple times a day, in the airspace with crewed fifth-gen fighters, other CCAs, starting to build that trust.”

David Alexander, president of General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, said that once a foundation has been built for Airmen to autonomously use CCAs and they are comfortable, the program can focus more on Agile Combat Employment operations, where aircraft are flown from smaller, potentially austere and isolated bases, without the same level of support a larger base might have.

At that point, Alexander said, “it’s not an experiment anymore, it’s an everyday event.”

Levin said those ACE exercises are vital, because that’s where operators find the shortcomings of CCA’s software. And if those problems aren’t rapidly fixed, he said, Airmen in the field won’t become comfortable using CCAs.

“When we go out to those ACE exercises and they don’t like something, if we don’t fix it by the next ACE, they’re not going to trust the system,” Levin said. “They’re not going to trust that it does what it needs to do.”

Anduril’s Fury in July fired its first weapon—an AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile—and General Atomics’ Vengeance will conduct its first live fire test later this year.

The biggest challenge that remains for the CCA concept, Bartlett said, is seeing whether their mission autonomy programming will deliver everything the Air Force needs and contractors have promised.

“Mission autonomy is going to be the secret sauce that lets these things become decisive or not, and we’ll know that over the next couple years, as that develops,” Bartlett said.

The Air Force has decades of established doctrine governing how it employs piloted fighters and other aircraft, Bartlett said, but the book for using CCAs is still being written. And as the Air Force figures out how it wants to use them, it needs to make sure this doctrine is tailor-made for CCAs and doesn’t just rehash existing guidelines.

“Working the nuances of CCA and fielding policies that are not just copy-pastes from old regulations, that are actually something that enables us to move quickly with these things … is, I think, our big challenge right now,” Bartlett said.

But it’s not just the Air Force that needs to adjust for a world with CCAs in it, Bartlett said. The entire nation will also have to get used to the concept of uncrewed aircraft regularly flying in U.S. airspace, he said. That will have policy implications, he said, and the Federal Aviation Administration will have to figure out how to integrate pilotless aircraft into the airspace it manages.

“Our system is not set up for that,” Bartlett said. The U.S. government has “to set policies that make sure the enterprise, and the country, is ready to receive these, and internalize an autonomous fighter that does not have a pilot, that is running on a mission autonomy agent, that doesn’t listen to” air traffic control.

items.title: MHS GENESIS Patient Portal transitioning to myAuth login Sept. 23
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: Throughout 2026, the online platforms that support your TRICARE benefit are switching from DS Logon to myAuth. myAuth is a simpler, more streamlined login authentication application. Many platforms, including milConnect, ID Card Office Online, and contractor portals, have already made this switch.
items.body:
Throughout 2026, the online platforms that support your TRICARE benefit are switching from DS Logon to myAuth . myAuth is a simpler, more streamlined login authentication application. Many platforms, including milConnect , ID Card Office Online , and contractor portals, have already made this switch.

On Sept. 23, the MHS GENESIS Patient Portal will make this switch. This means you’ll use myAuth to log in to MHS GENESIS Patient Portal to access health records from care at military hospitals and clinics .

When the transition to myAuth occurs, you’ll have multiple options for logging in . With myAuth, you can log in with:

A Common Access Card

A username/password, plus a secure multi-factor authentication method

Okta Verify. This is an app for personal or government mobile devices that enables secure access without a CAC.

How will this change happen?

When you log in to the patient portal after the transition, you'll see a new login page. This page will help you create a myAuth account if you don’t already have one. You can also visit myAuth for further instructions on creating an account.

What if I need help?

If you’re experiencing issues, visit myAuth Help for additional resources and guidance on creating or updating your account. You can also find answers to frequently asked questions . If you still need additional assistance, contact the Defense Manpower Data Center at 800-368-3665. DMDC manages myAuth and can answer questions about the transition or address any related concerns.

Although you’ll create a new login for myAuth, remember that neither TRICARE nor its contractors will contact you asking for private information like your date of birth, Social Security number, or your username and password. Read messages carefully and check the source email or web address for legitimacy. If something feels off, trust your instincts. If you think you gave personal or account information to a fraudulent entity, change your password right away and file a report .

In the end, the switch to myAuth means:

**Enhanced security:**More options to protect against unauthorized access

A modernized authentication platform: More ways to log in

**A more user-friendly experience:**A simpler interface

The switch to myAuth means a simpler, more secure experience in MHS GENESIS Patient Portal.

items.title: Faces of the Blue Diamond: U.S. Navy Petty Officer 2nd Class Josue Romero
items.author: LCpl Mia Ocampo
items.summary: Whether it’s patrolling the hills of Horno or conducting live-fire ranges, the readiness of an infantry division relies as much on cognitive resilience as it does on physical conditioning. For U.S. Navy Hospital Corpsman 2nd Class Josue Romero, a behavioral health technician with Headquarters Battalion, 1st Marine Division safeguarding that resilience is a full-time mission.
items.body:
Whether it’s patrolling the hills of Horno or conducting live-fire ranges, the readiness of an infantry division relies as much on cognitive resilience as it does on physical conditioning.

For U.S. Navy Hospital Corpsman 2nd Class Josue Romero, a behavioral health technician with Headquarters Battalion, 1st Marine Division safeguarding that resilience is a full-time mission.

Romero, a native of Nevada, assists medical providers with crisis interventions, patient intakes, follow-up evaluations and group therapy sessions. Working with 1st Marine Division units, Romero’s daily operational tempo shifts rapidly to meet operational demands, which may include conducting walk-in psychological evaluations for commands.

“We have the capability of going to different units and checking up on people, seeing how everything is functioning and showing them, ‘hey we’re here,’” Romero said. Romero views behavioral health as directly tied to combat readiness, emphasizing that untreated emotional and mental health concerns can affect a Marine’s physical performance, decision-making, and overall safety.

“Let’s say for example, they’re having sleep concerns for whatever reason, they haven’t been eating well, they’ve been depressed.,” Romero said. “Now you put this Marine in a 7-ton to conduct whatever training operation. They fall asleep behind the wheel, now they’re putting themselves and others at risk.” Embedded with Marines, Navy medical personnel frequently share the same field conditions as the Marines they support, eventually establishing a baseline of trust. Romero says he gains a deeper understanding of the Marines he serves through those shared experiences.

“Because we work so closely with Marines, we have that personal experience too. We understand what they’re going through.” Romero said. “Just knowing that they have somebody they can rely on, that they feel comfortable talking to about what they have going on is something that feels like no other. I take a lot of pride in that.” Romero encourages small-unit leaders and peers to look for signs of distress such as changes in hygiene, social isolation, irritability or decline in job performance. A persistent challenge is the stigma that seeking mental health support is a sign of personal or professional weakness. Romero urges Marines to not ignore their problems, but to view mental health concerns like a check-engine light. Whenever it does turn on, he wants Marines to know there are resources available. “Our doors are always open,” said Romero.

Marines and Sailors seeking confidential support can access installation resources through the Community Counseling Center, the Department of Defense inTransition program, or Military OneSource at 1-800-342-9647.

items.title: US Air Force to extend service of B-1, B-2 bombers, official says
items.author: Cristina Stassis
items.summary: The service lives of the B-1 Lancer and B-2 Spirit will be extended, with their pilots to be some of the first to fly the B-21 Raider.
items.body:
MilTech

US Air Force to extend service of B-1, B-2 bombers, official says

People photograph a U.S. Air Force B-1 as it approaches to land at RAF Fairford, Gloucestershire, Britain, March 17, 2026. (Toby Melville/Reuters)

Two of the U.S. Air Force’s bomber aircraft will be extended in an effort to better maintain the fleet’s readiness, a service official said Wednesday.

The decision to extend the B-1 Lancer and B-2 Spirit comes amid moves by the force to further develop the B-21 Raider, the service’s next-generation stealth bomber with accelerated production.

Both the bombers will be extended, Gen. Stephen L. Davis, commander of the Air Force Global Strike Command, said during a panel titled “Flying and Fixing to Fight and Win” at the Air & Space Forces Association’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference .

The commander said that the experienced pilots from the bombers will be some of the first B-21 pilots.

The Raiders are on track for a 2027 delivery to Ellsworth Air Force Base, South Dakota. The service aims to replace the aging B-1 and B-2 fleets in the coming decades with at least 100 B-21s.

Davis highlighted the Air Force’s Bomber Supplemental Trainer for Aircrew Readiness, or BSTAR , program, which is meant to address gaps and flight-hour readiness for B-1 pilots. In the program, XSTAR Aviation provides the force with HondaJet Elite light business jets.

“We’re bringing in a HondaJet to actually help experience some pilots, and also as some of these airframes have issues with readiness, it gives those pilots a chance to fly and get them time in the seat, which we know is very important,” Davis said during the panel.

The commander didn’t say how long the bombers’ service lives would be extended for, but the service intends to modernize and invest in the B-1 and B-2s in the coming years despite both aircraft being slated for retirement in the next decade.

Recently, the service launched an operation readiness campaign, dubbed the North Star Readiness Campaign , to increase the number of mission-capable B-52 Stratofortress and B-1s by accelerating the delivery of parts, engineering support and depot maintenance.

During the campaign’s announcement, the force said that while the B-22 and B-1 are being upgraded to continue service, the B-2 will be maintained for combat effectiveness until the B-21 is fully operational.

items.title: 673d Medical Group offers new 24-hour prescription refill option
items.author: A1C Thomas Polk
items.summary: The 673d Medical Group at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson now has a ScriptCenter Kiosk, providing users contactless access to refill prescriptions. While accessible to all, the automated kiosk will be of particular benefit to those working night and swing shifts, offering a modern and secure way for users to collect their prescriptions on their schedule.
items.body:
JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska – The 673d Medical Group at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson now has a ScriptCenter Kiosk, providing users contactless access to refill prescriptions. While accessible to all, the automated kiosk will be of particular benefit to those working night and swing shifts, offering a modern and secure way for users to collect their prescriptions on their schedule.

“The ScriptCenter Kiosk advances the JBER Ready Airman and Soldier mission by providing modern pharmaceutical capability and after-hours prescription access that is conducive to their work schedules,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Brian Johnson, commander of the 673d Medical Support Squadron.

The kiosk, located in the Emergency Department waiting area, houses 44 non-refrigerated lockers. Users can place refill orders in the Military Health System GENESIS Patient Portal. If requests are made for refridgerated medication they will be routed to a standard pharmacy, and the individual will be notified when it is available.

The ScriptCenter has been designed to make refilling prescriptions easy. In the MHS GENESIS Patient Portal under the Rx refill tab, users can select the ScriptCenter under the ‘choose a pharmacy’ option. There will be an initial sign-up process when first using the kiosk. Users will set up a four-digit PIN for secure access. When picking up an order it is recommended to bring military ID and the prescription number. The lockers are accessible to both active-duty members and their dependents with valid ID.

Airman 1st Class Rossukon Gonphila, pharmacy technician assigned to the 673d MDSS, has been leading the program at JBER. Gonphila highlighted the benefit of the system helping those who have difficulty accessing pharmacy services during business hours.

“Some operations have personnel working night shifts, or shifts where they can’t pick up during normal hours,” said Gonphila. “They have the opportunity to pick up at the ScriptCenter even after we are closed.”

items.title: SPACECOM Boss Wants Better Domain Awareness to Target Threats on Orbit
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: The Space Force revealed this week that it has space control weapons on orbit, but the head of U.S. Space Command said the U.S. still has “a long way to go” in improving its ability to detect and target threats in the domain. The post SPACECOM Boss Wants Better Domain Awareness to Target Threats on Orbit appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Space Force revealed this week that it has space control weapons on orbit , but the head of U.S. Space Command said the U.S. still has “a long way to go” in improving its ability to detect and target threats in the domain.

“To be able to negate threats in space, we must be able to find, fix, track, and target those threats,” SPACECOM Commander Gen. Stephen Whiting said Sept. 16 at the AMOS Conference in Maui, Hawaii. “Targeting in the space domain is maturing, but it still has a long way to go. We don’t have robust target folders like the joint force does in other domains.”

Space domain awareness , which is the military’s term for being able to see and understand what’s happening in the environment, is foundational for military operations on orbit. The better the data, the better decisions commanders can make about how to move through the domain and respond to threats that might impede that freedom of maneuver.

In a roundtable with reporters following his speech, Whiting said there has been some progress within the Space Force to improve the quality and quantity of its object tracking data. However, key shortfalls remain, and closing those gaps is a top priority for his command.

“Do I have all the track quality that I need at all times? No,” he said. “And that is why, in my current list of gaps that we every year go through a process to analyze, in my top five, we have a need for improved space domain awareness for space engagements.”

Whiting highlighted three examples of areas for improvement:

better integration of commercial and allied data

stronger linkages between sensors, command-and-and control systems, and effectors, including space weapons

expanded ground- and space-based surveillance capabilities

Whiting said that while data quality from both commercial industry and U.S. allies has improved significantly in recent years, integration issues and unstable funding have made it hard to take full advantage of those improvements.

“I want to be able to take commercial data, data from our allies, and get it into our programs of record today,” he said. “Right now, we can’t do that. We take that commercial and allied data and do an incredible job of processing it, but in a parallel way to our programs of record. We’ve got to be able to close those two together, for example, to make progress here.”

Fixing that integration challenge, he said, would represent “the biggest initial step we could take—and we could take that in the short term.”

Whiting also highlighted longstanding challenges around tying together the sensors that collect and process information, the C2 systems that analyze it, and the “effectors” that act on that intelligence. Combined, that string of systems makes up what’s called a “space kill chain,” and the Space Force has been focused on closing gaps in key parts of that architecture —many of them classified—for the past few years.

“We really need the acquisition organizations in the services who are delivering space domain awareness sensors, command and control systems, and effectors to work horizontally to make sure that we’re closing the kill chain by providing the space domain awareness target-quality track that the command and control systems and the effectors require to be effective,” he said. “We must be able to reach across all of these vertical program offices to make sure they deliver as an intact kill chain.”

Longer term, Whiting said, there’s a need for better surveillance of orbits beyond geosynchronous , to include cislunar pathways between the Earth and the moon.

“We want to see that scale beyond geosynchronous orbit … out to cislunar space and be able to maintain track of objects in those areas so that we’re not operationally surprised,” he said.
