items.title: A Calling to Serve, Interrupted
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: Before joining the Army in 2009, Sgt. 1st Class David Hong felt a deep calling to ministry. He found his purpose in the Army as a Religious Affairs Specialist – a role demanding that he constantly put the spiritual and emotional needs of his fellow Soldiers above his own. Since that time, he has dedicated nearly 17 years of his life to taking care of others.
items.body:
Fort Carson SRU: Rising Above . . . Finding a Way! (2007-2027) This is the second in a series of feature articles on the amazing Soldiers who have walked through the doors of the Fort Carson Soldier Recovery Unit and found success in their transition back to the force or civilian life. The series highlights the courage, perseverance, and resilience of those who have faced life-changing illnesses and injuries and found meaning and purpose as they continue to write the next chapter of their life story. These Soldiers, and the cadre and staff who supported them, leave an enduring legacy for good.

Featured Soldier: Sgt. 1st Class David Hong

Hometown: San Diego, California

Military Occupational Specialty (MOS): Religious Affairs Specialist (Chaplain’s Assistant)

By Sgt 1st Class Sebastien Fournier, Fort Carson Soldier Recovery Unit

Before joining the Army in 2009, Sgt. 1st Class David Hong felt a deep calling to ministry. He found his purpose in the Army as a Religious Affairs Specialist – a role demanding that he constantly put the spiritual and emotional needs of his fellow Soldiers above his own. Since that time, he has dedicated nearly 17 years of his life to taking care of others.

In July 2022, shortly after returning from a year-long deployment to Korea, Hong was serving as the senior Religious Affairs NCO for the Fort Carson garrison. Approaching 50 and navigating a demanding operational tempo, he followed a physician’s recommendation to get a routine screening colonoscopy.

The results were devastating. Doctors discovered a severe blockage and diagnosed him with stage IV colon cancer.

"To be honest with you, if I didn't get that colonoscopy, I would probably not be here talking to you," Hong reflected.

Initially, Hong tried to push through, attempting to balance his demanding military duties with his first grueling rounds of chemotherapy. The physical toll was immense, and it quickly became apparent that he needed a dedicated environment to fight for his life. In September 2023, his First Sergeant gave him a direct order: it was time to transition to the Fort Carson Soldier Recovery Unit.

The Turning Point: Learning to be a Patient Transitioning to the SRU required a monumental shift in mindset. For a senior NCO accustomed to leading and caring for troops, stepping back was the ultimate challenge.

"Not being able to do my job as a Religious Affairs NCO was the hardest thing," Hong explained. "It took me almost a year to accept that I had to focus on being a patient. I learned self-care here, which is hard for NCOs because we're used to taking care of others."

Once assigned to the SRU, Hong was met with a comprehensive, synchronized care network. From nurse case managers and social workers to squad leaders and the command team, administrative and logistical burdens were lifted off his shoulders.

This support proved vital as he endured more than 30 rounds of chemotherapy, a major liver resection surgery in April 2024, and the demands of family life, which includes caring for a special needs child.

"I remember one of the battalion commanders called me while I was sitting in the chair getting ready for surgery and said, 'Hey sergeant, we're praying for you, just hang in there,'" Hong recalled. "That was huge. Having the team and resources made it easier to go through the treatments and transitions."

The Discipline to Pursue an Ambitious Dream While at the SRU, Hong was introduced to adaptive sports through the Army Recovery Care Program. Despite the debilitating effects of long-term oncology care, he committed to an intense, bi-weekly schedule that alternated chemotherapy infusions with high-performance training.

Because chemotherapy left Hong severely immunocompromised, Coach Colin at Fort Carson’s Garcia Gym adapted to protect his health, opening the facility an hour early, allowing Hong to train safely in isolation before other athletes arrived. When scheduling racing chair track sessions became difficult around infusion dates, Hong adapted by using the ski ergometer to simulate stroke mechanics.

Navigating heavy physical training under intense chemotherapy required a strict, targeted nutritional regimen. Hong credits his wife Monica as his de facto nutritionist. She developed a disciplined, organic plant-based protocol, handled daily juicing, raw food prep, and the logistics of specialized meals at home and on the road. Eventually he added in some protein such as fish but completed the bulk of his training fully vegan.

Warrior Games: Defying the Odds Hong’s disciplined regimen earned his spot to represent Team Army at the Department of Defense Warrior Games in both 2025 and 2026. He competed in an exhaustive roster of events across multiple disciplines, to include track and field in recumbent racing chair events, seated shot put, and seated discus, cycling, archery, and sitting volleyball.

"Training while doing treatment was very difficult, but having the support made it easier," Hong said. "It's not about medaling; it's about being part of that community. Track and field was the most challenging because I did every single event... It was a complete team effort across all service branches, supported by great coaches and cadre."

Positivity, Gratitude, and Enduring Service Throughout his tenure at the SRU, Hong became known across the battalion for his unwavering optimism, radiant joy, and selfless concern for others. When asked where his resilience originates in the face of a terminal diagnosis, Hong points directly to his spiritual foundation.

"Personally, it’s my faith in God. Even with a terminal illness, I try not to be bitter. Treatment isn't fun, but you have to stay positive, love the people around you, and encourage others," Hong stated. "I’m not the only one going through struggles. Cancer is horrible, but I look at the positive aspects and see how God is using this journey as a testimony to help others overcome their challenges. I didn't do this on my own—God used the SRU, the doctors, and everyone I’ve encountered along the way."

In June 2026, Hong was medically retired from active military service. Facing the reality of a terminal illness, his focus has shifted to maximizing time with his family – to include his three daughters and one grandson. As his condition eventually progresses, his wife will step into the role of his primary caregiver.

Despite all of that, Hong's desire to serve remains as strong as ever. Grateful for the support he received from his entire care team at the SRU, Hong feels a calling to spend some of his remaining time volunteering to help connect transitioning veterans with adaptive sports and other critical resources.

"The legacy I want to leave is that anybody can do what we did as athletes," Hong emphasized. "Even though you're going through treatment, if you have the right support like this SRU, you're able to train... It gives me a vision that as I transition to civilian life, I still want to support Soldiers, their families, and veterans."

About the Fort Carson SRU T he Fort Carson SRU opened its doors on June 2, 2007, as one of 45 Warrior Transition Units stood up during the peak of catastrophic casualties from the Global War on Terror. Today, Fort Carson is one of 14 remaining Soldier Recovery Units that have served and supported the Army’s wounded, ill and injured Soldiers for almost two decades. Due to the continued decrease in demand and increasing capability to remotely manage less complex medical cases, Fort Carson along with 9 other SRUs will close in 2027.

The Fort Carson SRU has served more than 4,500 Soldiers in Recovery. Almost 500 Soldiers have returned to Active Duty and continued to serve, with another 600 Reservists and National Guard members returning to their units. Another 3,300 have transitioned to civilian life.

items.title: COMAMC emphasizes air mobility’s role in ‘Flying and Fixing to Fight and Win’ at AFA 2026
items.author: 1st Lt. Kevin Powers
items.summary: Lt. Gen. Daniel Tulley, commander of Air Mobility Command, joined fellow commanders and senior leaders to address service members, defense industry partners and journalists during the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space and Cyber Conference, Sept. 16.
items.body:
Lt. Gen. Daniel Tulley, commander of Air Mobility Command, joined fellow commanders and senior leaders to address service members, defense industry partners and journalists during the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space and Cyber Conference, Sept. 16.

Tulley joined Gen. S. L. Davis , commander of Air Force Global Strike Command, Lt. Gen. Linda Hurry, commander of Air Force Materiel Command and Maj. Gen. Jon Eberlan, Director of Logistics, Engineering and Force Protection, Headquarters Air Combat Command, for a panel discussion focused on the Chief of Staff of the Air Force's operational imperative to fly and fix aircraft to deter adversaries and, if deterrence fails, to fight and win decisively in contested theaters.

Addressing the current tempo of operations, Tulley highlighted that Air Mobility Command has roughly 300 aircraft deployed across several geographic combatant commands, supported by approximately 10,000 Airmen operating at an intense tempo. He stressed that strategic air refueling is only a fraction of the total support required to sustain the Joint Force. AMC also delivers the supplies, the munitions, the sustainment and the base operating support that combatant commanders count on.

"Air refueling is just part of the story," Tulley said. "What strikes me is the lessons that they're bringing back. We've got a generation of Airmen who are going to come back home with combat experience that will be priceless for [countering] our pacing threat."

When asked about managing readiness with a largely fixed inventory of aircraft, Tulley challenged legacy, binary models of preparedness, advocating for systems that measure combat capability in a protracted fight.

"When we think about readiness in Air Mobility Command, we really think about answering four questions: readiness of what, for what, for when, and at what cost. But when we look at the lessons in Ukraine, we also have to ask ourselves: for how long?" Tulley stated. "Readiness in contact is the way we're approaching this."

To illustrate the joint teamwork required to generate readiness in contact, Tulley noted that AFMC pushed forward depot-level capabilities to Royal Air Force Mildenhall, United Kingdom, where maintenance teams have successfully swapped 30 KC-135 Stratotanker boom assemblies in-theater rather than flying the aircraft back to the United States for repairs.

Turning to the challenges of concurrent global demand and operating across multiple theaters, Tulley explained that AMC functions as the global air component to U.S. Transportation Command, balancing requirements across 11 combatant commands.

"For us, it's really about discerning the requirements across those combatant commands to include TRANSCOM's own, and then their priorities," Tulley explained. "What we really need, and what we're moving towards, is a system that lets us see all 11 combatant commands."

Addressing the pilot pipeline and training constraints, Tulley emphasized that the command is looking at the entire enterprise to ensure experienced aircrews are in operational squadrons.

"At the end of the day, we really need experience in the squadrons," Tulley said, noting that he recently convened a team to examine how the command can simplify its training requirements. "How much time do we spend in training now? What are our requirements for all of our mission sets. How can we simplify that? Always assure we have the basic level of readiness to keep the global transportation system operating, but then tailor the training we need for that high-end fight."

To highlight the reality of operating and fixing aircraft while under fire, Tulley recounted a recent real-world mission where a KC-135 aircrew and maintenance team sheltered during a ballistic missile attack, then immediately emerged to contain a major fuel leak, patch shrapnel holes and repair the aircraft so it could complete a transoceanic flight home for depot restoration. Tulley stressed that readiness is a vital, continuous process for the command.

"Pretty simple for us: train like you fight, train like you will fight in a peer fight," Tulley said. "Training like you fight has got to stress our Airmen. It’s got to train them to be ready for those stresses, and then do it again and again and again."

Tulley concluded by discussing the evolution of contested logistics, highlighting that AMC has adapted to track detailed replacement parts for aircraft in contested theaters, alongside combat munitions shipments.

"One of the things I'd say about logistics and supply lines are that we are good, but we're getting better," Tulley stated. "If you can get to the granularity and the precision to say, 'Okay, I need these [Mission Impaired Capability Awaiting Parts] delivered with those munitions,' you're increasing combat capability. You're turning aircraft back into the fight faster."

As AMC continues to operate at a sustained global tempo, Tulley emphasized that the command’s advantage rests on its ability to generate, sustain and regenerate combat capability under contested conditions. By integrating maintenance, logistics, training and operational planning across the mobility enterprise, AMC is working to ensure its Airmen and aircraft can support the Joint Force wherever and whenever they are needed.

items.title: Blount Island team tests new Navy option for moving fuel ashore
items.author: Dustin Senger
items.summary: Steven Insco, a test coordinator supporting Blount Island Command, worked through a verification checklist Sept. 16, then started a pump-and-compressor configuration designed to give military planners another way to move fuel and water to forces ashore.
items.body: ST. MARYS, Ga. — Steven Insco, a test coordinator supporting Blount Island Command, worked through a verification checklist Sept. 16, then started a pump-and-compressor configuration designed to give military planners another way to move fuel and water to forces ashore. The equipment ran at several settings as Navy acquisition, engineering and logistics specialists observed and documented its performance. The pump and compressor operated outside the compact container intended to house them, allowing evaluators to focus on the stand-alone pumping configuration. The Navy calls the new configuration the Amphibious Bulk Liquid Transfer System-J, or ABLTS-J. The “J” refers to Joint Logistics Over-the-Shore. Blount Island Command’s Navy positioning specialists at Marine Corps Support Facility Blount Island in Florida developed it to complement — not replace or supersede — the fielded ABLTS. ABLTS uses hose lines to transfer bulk fuel or water from a ship to shore. When employed from a maritime prepositioning ship, the system relies on pumping support from the vessel. ABLTS-J would place that pumping capability in a transportable package, giving commanders more flexibility to employ the transfer system from different platforms and locations. “We’re good — we’ve proved the concept,” said William Fish, director of Blount Island Command’s Navy positioning department. “We know it’ll fit dimensionally. Now we just need to operate it in the container.” Mike Prouty, principal assistant program manager for the Navy’s Joint Petroleum Over-the-Shore effort, traveled from the Washington Navy Yard to a coastal Georgia industrial yard to observe the test. He said ABLTS-J grew from an engineering change proposal for a stand-alone configuration. “We’re happy with what we’re seeing — excited by what we’re seeing — but we still have some steps left,” Prouty said. After Blount Island Command completes the containerized configuration, the program plans to move ABLTS-J to fleet demonstrations in an operational environment. Prouty’s program falls within PMS 300H, which manages the Navy’s Logistics Over-the-Shore portfolio under the Boats and Craft Program Office of Portfolio Acquisition Executive Maritime. The portfolio brings together capabilities for moving equipment, cargo, personnel and bulk fuel from ships to shore when conventional port infrastructure is unavailable or unsuitable. For Blount Island Command, the project connects the workforce’s positioning mission with the Navy’s future sustainment requirements, turning familiarity with existing equipment into options for the fleet. Insco brought a fleet operator’s experience to the evaluation. He retired as a Navy chief petty officer after 20 years as a boatswain’s mate, including small-boat operations in coastal and near-shore environments. “We’re taking a fielded system traditionally employed from maritime prepositioning ships and giving it a stand-alone pumping option,” Fish said. “We want to make ABLTS operable anywhere in the world, from any barge or remote island.” Before the field evaluation, participants met at Marine Corps Support Facility Blount Island to review design constraints and timelines, set development priorities, assign engineering and logistics responsibilities and discuss potential updates to Navy training curricula. With the pumping concept established, the team will modify a compact shipping container to house and operate the pump-and-compressor package while accounting for ventilation, heat, vibration and access to the controls. The design is also intended to limit modifications required in the field. A Naval Sea Logistics Center representative observed the kickoff and field test to identify requirements for training, repair parts and technical manuals, while a naval architect documented observations to help finalize the system drawings. The ABLTS-J effort follows a pattern at Blount Island Command. The command provides equipment, space and expertise for autonomous-navigation testing aboard an Improved Navy Lighterage System causeway ferry. In June, it revised a loading plan aboard USNS Sgt. William R. Button to accommodate a causeway ferry while creating space for additional containers. Across those projects, the command brought engineers, logisticians and experienced operators together to develop more workable options for the fleet. That problem-solving pattern also helps explain why Fish’s team accepted the ABLTS-J work despite an already demanding workload. Blount Island Command’s Navy specialists sustain, configure and position maritime logistics equipment and supplies. Their familiarity with how systems are stored, transported, maintained and prepared for forward employment made developing the configuration a natural extension of their daily mission. “We’re saturated with work, but where else you going to do it?” Fish said. “We’re trying like hell to produce a good product, and in the end we will.”

items.title: Pentagon, Lockheed to Expand Production of Secretive New Joint Advanced Tactical Missile
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: The Pentagon announced a deal with Lockheed Martin on Sept. 17 to expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, an advanced new Air Force and Navy air-to-air missile meant to equip fifth- and sixth-generation fighters. The post Pentagon, Lockheed to Expand Production of Secretive New Joint Advanced Tactical Missile appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Pentagon announced a deal with Lockheed Martin on Sept. 17 to expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, an advanced new Air Force and Navy air-to-air missile meant to equip fifth- and sixth-generation fighters.

The “framework” agreement aims to give Lockheed a “long-term demand” signal, part of a push by President Donald Trump’s administration to build and sustain a more robust munitions manufacturing industrial base.

The announcement “establishes the framework for future multiyear procurement of JATM,” according to the Pentagon release.

“We will deliver JATM at the speed our nation and allies demand while providing value for taxpayers and our shareholders,” Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed Missiles and Fire Control, said in a company release .

A Lockheed spokesperson declined to answer further questions from Air & Space Forces Magazine, deferring to the Department of Defense. A Pentagon press officer also declined any further comment about the announcement.

The announcement should signal to Lockheed and other munitions-makers that a stable market is taking shape, said Mark Gunzinger, director of future concepts and capability assessments at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies.

“It is difficult for industry to justify expenditures needed to accelerate and scale up production,” the retired Air Force colonel said. “This is a key reason why this is an important framework.”

Next-Gen Option

The JATM is the successor to the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, which has been in service since 1991.

The radar-guided, medium-range, supersonic AMRAAM has undergone major upgrades since its inception, most recently in 2020. The F-22 Raptor, F-35 Lightning II, F-15 Eagle variants, and the F-16 Fighting Falcon can all carry it, and the Air Force isn’t looking to stop buying the missile even as it looks to the JATM.

The service is seeking $953 million for 618 AMRAAMs in its fiscal 2027 budget request, while the Navy is asking for $673 million to buy 388 AMRAAMs.

The JATM seeks to overmatch the Chinese military’s PL-15 and PL-17 missiles and will reportedly double the AMRAAM’s range and hit targets in excess of 120 miles away, though much of its capabilities have been shrouded in secrecy for years.

In its fiscal 2026 budget request, the Air Force revealed it had bought 144 JATMs in 2024-2025 and planned to buy at least another 112 missiles. The fiscal 2027 request, still pending before Congress, has $1.5 billion in procurement to scale up production, but budget documents don’t list any quantities.

While upgraded AMRAAMs provide an improved strike option for fighter aircraft, the JATM is necessary for advanced aircraft already fielded and those in the pipeline, such as the F-47 and Collaborative Combat Aircraft variants, the FQ-42 Vengeance and FQ-44 Fury.

“It doesn’t make sense to invest in highly survivable and incredibly capable fifth- and sixth-gen fighters and bombers just to saddle them with payloads of weapons that will not survive to reach their targets in a fight with a peer adversary,” Gunzinger said.

Mix for the Future Fight

Though reports on the current conflict with Iran don’t indicate the U.S. is using large numbers of air-to-air missiles, a future conflict with a peer adversary such as the Chinese military is likely to look much different.

“Multiple Mitchell Institute wargames have spotlighted the need to rapidly grow the U.S. Air Force’s inventory of advanced air-to-air weapons, which could be nearly depleted within a couple of weeks of high-intensity combat with a peer adversary,” Gunzinger said.

This isn’t the first time the Pentagon has announced plans for multiyear procurement of key missiles.

In July, the Pentagon announced a similar framework for a USAF program known as the Family of Affordable Mass Munitions, which will produce lower-cost cruise missiles that experts believe will be needed in future conflicts for higher strike volumes.

That deal anticipates 8,000 missiles annually once production is at full strength. Work is expected to ramp up by 2028 with 5,300 missiles produced, increasing to the 8,000-missile mark by 2031.

While the FAMM deal will bulk up low-cost options for the Air Force, work on more expensive but more capable munitions are an important part of the equation.

“Our air forces will have a future high-low mix of counter-air weapons, but it’s far more important to focus on the cost to achieve an effect in the battlespace like countering an enemy air threat than the unit cost of a weapon,” Gunzinger said. “The key is to determine the right high-low mix based on optimizing cost per effect instead of simply chasing lower unit costs.”

Allies and Partner Purchases

The U.S. isn’t the only country interested in JATM—Australia announced $736 million in spending to equip its Royal Australian Air Force with the weapon.

That move, along with potential deals with other allies and partners, could also help reduce missile costs for the U.S.

“I believe sharing production with key allies as soon as possible is critical to improving their interoperability with U.S. air forces and lead to cost-sharing agreements that can accelerate weapon development and acquisition,” Gunzinger said.

Beyond cost savings, having allies buy the next-generation missile for their fleets also gives the U.S. ways to standardize weapons loaders across a coalition and share munitions when needed, he said.

items.title: The US Army is looking for new drones to ferry blood supplies
items.author: Michael Peck
items.summary: As part of the U.S. Army Blood Link project, the service is seeking new drones that can transport blood supplies in the field.
items.body:
MilTech

The US Army is looking for new drones to ferry blood supplies

Soldiers change the batteries of a drone during a drone-based blood resupply as part of the multinational Hospital Exercise. (Sgt. Jose Lora/Army)

The U.S. Army is looking for drones that can transport blood supplies in the field, according to a new sources sought notice from the service.

The Army aims to select a contractor that can deliver two prototype UAVs for what it is calling the Army Blood Link project, the notice states. Each drone must be capable of transporting 20 units of blood products.

The deadline to respond to the notice is Sept. 21, and the drones will need to be delivered within three months of the contract award.

“Due to the compressed timeline, we recommend focusing on further development and adaptation of existing commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) UAS solutions,” the notice emphasized.

The request for proposals, issued on behalf of the XVIII Airborne Corps Joint Operations Innovation Outpost, calls for a UAV that can haul a minimum of 35 pounds and up to 50 pounds. The drone should have a one-way transport radius of 30 kilometers and a maximum range of 100 kilometers, the notice states.

Maximum speed was not specified in the request, but the Army wants a UAV capable of flying at an altitude of up to 18,000 feet. The request notes that the UAV should also be capable of a “maximum 30-minute response time from mission request to launch under standard operating conditions.”

Given the perishability of blood supplies, the drone must carefully regulate its operating temperature, the Army requested. The cargo container should “maintain required temperature for up to [three] hours of transport time, within an ambient environment of 15°F to 120°F with high humidity,” the notice states.

The Army estimates a total mission duration of three to six hours, with blood carried within temperature limits for no more than three hours.

The request also details that the container must accommodate blood bags roughly 8 inches long and 5 inches wide. The cargo bay should also be resistant to vibration, rain, sand, chemical contamination and other environmental hazards.

Upon delivery, the drone will need to precisely land a cargo within 10 meters of the desired location, according to the request.

Potentially dropping of the blood supplies from the air is also possible, the notice states. This would mean a “drop capability from 10 to 15 meters above ground level with landing accuracy sufficient to remain within the 10-meter delivery-location requirement and not damage the blood products or compromise container integrity,” the request notes.

The Army envisions a semi-autonomous drone with “autonomous waypoint navigation and return-to-base functions, under operator supervision.” The service wants the UAV and its ground equipment to also have an operational lifespan of 500 to 1,500 flight hours.

The Army has been devoting more attention to the challenge of delivering blood supplies to the front lines. In May 2025, the 173rd Airborne Brigade used drones to transport blood during the Swift Response exercise in Lithuania.

Michael Peck is a correspondent for Defense News and a columnist for the Center for European Policy Analysis. He holds an M.A. in political science from Rutgers University. Find him at theuncommondefense.com. His email is mikedefense1@gmail.com.

items.title: Lockheed Martin gets first batch of Patriot interceptor parts from General Motors
items.author: Mike Stone, Reuters
items.summary: In an "extraordinary" 22-day turnaround, Lockheed Martin received its first shipment of critical components from General Motors for Patriot interceptors.
items.body:
Industry

Lockheed Martin gets first batch of Patriot interceptor parts from General Motors

A general view of a part of the Patriot missile system before it was transported to Poland from Gnoien, Germany, on Jan. 23, 2023. (Annegret Hilse/Reuters)

Lockheed Martin said on Thursday it received its first shipment of critical components from General Motors for Patriot interceptors , less than a month after the two companies inked a manufacturing agreement, as the Pentagon pushes for faster weapons production .

The ⁠Patriot missile defense system remains one of the world’s most sought-after weapons for the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and Russia’s prolonged war with Ukraine.

Since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Kyiv credits Patriot batteries with helping defend cities against Russian ballistic missile attacks, while Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has repeatedly appealed for ⁠more ​launchers and interceptors as Moscow intensifies air strikes.

GM Defense delivered the initial batch of housing components for the Patriot interceptors called the PAC-3 MSE — on Aug. 28, just 22 days after the Aug. 6 contract signing, Lockheed said, for parts that traditionally take months or years to produce.

The deal builds on a broader collaboration the two companies announced in June, when they said they were partnering to strengthen the U.S. defense industrial base amid surging demand for munitions, tapping GM Defense’s manufacturing plants and laboratories to boost production capacity and supply chain resilience.

“This extraordinary 22-day turnaround underscores Lockheed Martin’s relentless focus on execution — delivering for our troops faster, with greater capacity,” said Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control.

GM Defense President and CEO Stephen duMont said the automaker’s precision-fabrication expertise would support “production of this country’s critical defense capabilities.”

Lockheed is investing $8 billion to $9 billion to scale munitions output, including PAC-3 MSE, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) and the Precision Strike Missile (PrSM), adding new buildings and jobs at more than 20 U.S. sites. The company said production and warehousing space would grow nearly 50% following planned expansions.

items.title: Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms laboratory earns CAP, AABB reaccreditations
items.author: Christopher Jones
items.summary: Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms recognized its Laboratory Department Sept. 17, 2026, following recent reaccreditations by the College of American Pathologists (CAP) and the Association for the Advancement of Blood and Biotherapies (AABB). The two-year reaccreditations recognize the laboratory’s commitment to quality, accuracy and reliability across diagnostic testing, blood banking and transfusion services, which provide clinicians with critical information and capabilities to deliver high-quali
items.body:
TWENTYNINE PALMS, Calif. — Behind many of the medical decisions made at Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms is a team providing clinicians with the diagnostic information they need to deliver timely, high-quality care.

The Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms laboratory department recently earned reaccreditation from the College of American Pathologists (CAP), while its blood bank was also reaccredited by the Association for the Advancement of Blood and Biotherapies (AABB). Both accreditations are valid for two years.

Capt. Janiese Cleckley, director, Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms, presented the reaccreditation certificates to the laboratory team during a ceremony at the hospital on Sept. 17.

For Lt. Cmdr. Nathan Magare, director for clinical support services (DCSS) at Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms, the achievements reflect not only the quality of the laboratory, but the important role clinical support services play in delivering comprehensive healthcare and maintaining warfighter readiness.

“Lab services are critical in guiding clinicians’ decision making,” Magare said. “Lab diagnostics are the foundational engine of modern healthcare. Whether identifying infectious pathogens, monitoring chronic conditions, or screening for environmental-related injuries in the High Desert, our laboratory provides clinicians with the rapid, objective data required to make precise, definitive treatment decisions.”

The hospital's CAP accreditation encompasses a broad range of laboratory services, including bacteriology, chemistry, coagulation, hematology, immunohematology, point-of-care testing, special chemistry, toxicology, transfusion services, urinalysis and virology.

Those capabilities are especially important at Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center (MCAGCC) Twentynine Palms, where service members routinely conduct physically demanding training in a challenging desert environment.

“For warfighters executing rigorous combined-arms training at MCAGCC Twentynine Palms, precise and timely lab results directly support force survivability and combat readiness,” Magare said.

As DCSS, Magare helps oversee services that support providers throughout the continuum of patient care. While patients may most often associate healthcare with their direct interaction with a physician, nurse or corpsman, clinical support departments provide many of the diagnostic and therapeutic capabilities those providers rely on to evaluate patients and determine appropriate treatment.

The laboratory is a key part of that system, producing information that can help clinicians identify illness, monitor a patient's condition and guide treatment. Its blood bank and transfusion capabilities provide another critical component of care.

CAP accreditation requires laboratories to meet standards designed to promote accurate and reliable laboratory testing. Magare said reaccreditation provides independent validation of the laboratory's processes and the quality controls behind the results clinicians use to make medical decisions.

“CAP reaccreditation is the global gold standard for laboratory quality assurance,” Magare said. “It independently confirms that our specimen processing, calibration precision, and test reliability mirror those of top-tier academic medical centers, ensuring maximum diagnostic accuracy.”

For patients and healthcare providers, those standards mean the same emphasis on quality extends beyond the main hospital.

“This recognition assures warfighters, families, and providers that regardless of whether a specimen is drawn at the main hospital or a branch health clinic, the result meets identical national-tier quality controls under our HRO (high reliability organization) framework,” Magare said.

The laboratory's recent AABB reaccreditation further recognizes the standards maintained within its blood banking and transfusion operations. Together, the two reaccreditations demonstrate the breadth of quality controls supporting laboratory and transfusion services across the command.

Magare credited the accomplishments to the laboratory personnel who maintain those standards every day.

“This achievement reflects the relentless technical competence, discipline, and attention to detail demonstrated daily by our civilian and active-duty medical laboratory technicians, officers, and superb lab leadership,” Magare said. “Every CAP-certified result represents strict calibration, documentation, and peer review.”

That consistency, he added, is what makes accreditation more than a periodic inspection or administrative milestone.

“Reaccreditation is not the result of a temporary surge in effort; it reflects a daily culture of self-critique, peer accountability, and ongoing refinement that ensures our patients receive quality lab services around the clock,” Magare said.

For Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms, maintaining accredited clinical support capabilities helps ensure providers have the resources and information necessary to care for service members, retirees and families while supporting the readiness of the operational forces training at the installation.

“Operating aboard the Marine Corps’ premier desert training installation, our clinicians rely on laboratory accuracy to make critical medical decisions for warfighters under demanding conditions,” Magare said. “This milestone proves that our hospital consistently provides national-tier diagnostic reliability to our Marines, Sailors, retirees, allied nation service members and their families.”

items.title: US Navy should target carriers in fight with China, report says
items.author: Michael Peck
items.summary: A U.S. think tank devised a strategy to target Chinese aircraft carriers by using similar tactics that China has planned against American ships.
items.body:
Asia Pacific

US Navy should target carriers in fight with China, report says

In this photo released by Xinhua News Agency, China's third conventionally powered aircraft carrier, the Fujian, conducts a maiden sea trial on May 7, 2024. (Ding Ziyu/Xinhua via AP)

China is devoting enormous efforts — from submarines to ballistic missiles — to destroy America’s aircraft carriers.

The strategy prompted a U.S. think tank to ask why America couldn’t do the same and sink China’s growing fleet of carriers.

The think tank, the Center for Strategic and International Studies, devised a plan to target Chinese carriers by using many of the same tactics that China would use against American flattops.

“China’s expanding carrier force presents a strategic vulnerability that the United States and its allies can exploit, rather than merely a challenge to U.S. dominance,” argues a CSIS report , titled “Flip the Script.”

“Instead of treating U.S. carriers as hunted platforms, focusing on how to defend U.S. assets, this report argues that the United States and allied Pacific powers can — and should — go on the offense, becoming the hunters instead of the hunted in this near-peer competition,” it continues.

For years, China has painted a bullseye on American carriers, including building a full-sized mockup of a U.S. carrier in the Taklamakan Desert. Beyond the poetic justice of replying in kind, targeting Chinese carriers exploits the same sensitivities that Americans have about their vessels.

Just as losing a Ford-class carrier would deeply humiliate Washington, sinking a Fujian-class carrier would be devastating for Beijing. Just as U.S. planners must be cautious about committing carriers in waters exposed to submarine attack, so, too, might Chinese admirals.

“These platforms are both prestige projects and critical enablers of future Chinese sea control and expeditionary operations,” CSIS said. “Moreover, just like their U.S. counterparts, the Chinese carriers are high‑value, hard‑to‑replace assets vulnerable to long‑range strike.”

China currently has three operational aircraft carriers, and a 2025 Pentagon study estimated that the People’s Liberation Army Navy will build six more by 2035. Yet, Beijing’s quest to build a carrier fleet may be driven less by military considerations than by prestige, just as Britain and Germany raced to build dreadnoughts before the First World War.

“China’s desire to be taken seriously as a first‑rate power may drive its construction of these capital ships more than pure military thinking,” the CSIS report said. Thus, “the PLAN’s new carriers become concentrated nodes of military, political, and symbolic risk.”

The tactics advocated by CSIS may seem eerily familiar to U.S. Navy strategists contemplating American carriers sailing within harm’s way to save Taiwan from invasion. For example, CSIS envisions deploying manned and unmanned submarines that could ambush Chinese flattops. This would include U.S. nuclear subs and quiet diesel-electric boats from allies such as Australia, Japan and South Korea.

“The key is to turn the undersea domain into a continuous threat envelope that forces Beijing to invest heavily in escorts, ASW aviation, and fixed sensors simply to move carriers out of its home waters,” the report said.

Just like China and its “carrier-killer” ballistic missiles, the U.S. and its allies would deploy land-based missiles against Chinese ships, the CSIS plan says.

Launched from bases in Japan down to the Philippines, these weapons would interdict chokepoints that a Chinese carrier would be forced to pass through. The idea is that “the mere expectation that upon entering the Philippine Sea, carriers such as the Fujian or Sichuan will face dense, land‑based anti‑ship fires backed by allied ISR [reconnaissance and targeting] raises the perceived risk of using them as front‑line tools of coercion.”

In addition, the U.S. would target Chinese carriers with air-launched, anti-ship missiles backed by satellite surveillance. Meanwhile, electronic and cyber warfare would disrupt Chinese command networks in the same way that China would disrupt America’s.

Taking a leaf from Ukraine’s successful campaign to drive the Russian Navy out of the Black Sea, swarms of unmanned surface vessels would hit Chinese ports and ships in those ports.

“The central idea is to make a carrier’s routine employment around Taiwan, the South China Sea, or beyond the first island chain appear prohibitively risky, day in and day out,” said the report.

Historically, powerful and prestigious warships have been a double-edged sword. For example, in World War I and World War II, the German navy’s battleships and battlecruisers spent much of their time in port. Losing a capital ship — such as the battleship Bismarck in May 1941 — could be seen as a national humiliation.

“The potential domestic political fallout from losing the carriers might make the CCP [Chinese Communist Party] more risk-averse,” one U.S. expert on China told Defense News.

“The CCP spent a lot of political capital making its case to the public about building a carrier fleet,” said the expert, who spoke about the situation on the condition of anonymity. “The sustained public campaign to drum up support was part of a larger effort to shape China’s ‘maritime consciousness.’ The CCP tapped into naval nationalism to mobilize enormous resources for the buildup.”

The question then becomes what resources the U.S. Navy would need to threaten China’s carriers.

CSIS’s plan would require changes to U.S. defense strategy, especially building more submarines.

However, the study questioned whether U.S. shipyards have the capacity to build enough nuclear attack submarines to “sustain a dense ‘ambush belt’ against PLAN carrier groups.”

CSIS sees the solution as threefold: buying more unmanned underwater vehicles, investing in allied bases to host naval drones and procuring more torpedoes to bolster an inadequate stockpile.

Significantly, the plan calls for a change in the composition of the U.S. Navy. Rather than current plans for a force of 350 manned vessels and 150 surface and underwater drones, the force would be evenly split between 300 manned and 300 unmanned vessels under the CSIS plan.

The U.S. Army and Marine Corps would contribute units equipped with anti-ship missiles. The U.S. would also arrange for its Pacific allies to co-produce guided munitions.

“The United States cannot afford to fight a long war in the Western Pacific if every LRASM, SM‑6, or Naval Strike Missile must be produced in and shipped from North America,” CSIS said.

Beyond finding a means to discomfit China, the study seems to aim at critics who believe the U.S. Navy’s carriers have become a liability in the age of missiles and drones. CSIS argues that while U.S. carriers are not invulnerable, they “may not be as vulnerable as analysts assume.”

The “current discussion in Washington often frames carriers as unique to the United States and uniquely vulnerable, while underplaying the fact that China is now building its own large‑deck, network‑enabled capital ships that are at least as targetable as the U.S. ships China aims to threaten.”

Michael Peck is a correspondent for Defense News and a columnist for the Center for European Policy Analysis. He holds an M.A. in political science from Rutgers University. Find him at theuncommondefense.com. His email is mikedefense1@gmail.com.

items.title: Pentagon, Lockheed sign framework deal to boost AIM-260 production
items.author: Michael Scanlon
items.summary: The agreement was signed to expand production of the AIM-260 JATM, laying the groundwork for a future multiyear buy of the long-range air-to-air weapon.
items.body:
Pentagon

Pentagon, Lockheed sign framework deal to boost AIM-260 production

U.S. Marines load F/A-18 Hornet jets with an AIM-120, which will enventually be replaced by JATM, during a harpoon exercise at Marine Corps Air Station Iwakuni, Japan, Aug. 19, 2026. (Donald Dugger/U.S. Marine Corps)

The U.S. Defense Department and Lockheed Martin signed a framework agreement on Thursday to expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, or JATM, laying the groundwork for a future multiyear buy of the classified long-range air-to-air weapon.

The agreement is neither a contract nor an order for missiles. Officials described it as a demand signal to Lockheed and its suppliers to justify investing in capacity, workforce and production efficiencies. Should Congress authorize and fund a multiyear buy, the aim is for production lines to be ready when orders arrive.

“Speed, scale, and stability drive acquisition excellence, and these gears must turn in unison,” Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael Duffey said in the release. “Today’s announcement reflects our commitment to sending clear, long-term demand signals across the defense industrial base.”

Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control, said the company will invest its own money to expand capacity in advance of any orders.

“JATM is one of our nation’s most important air dominance capabilities, but because of the classified nature of the program, it’s also a story we haven’t been able to tell,” Cahill said in a statement reported by Reuters . “We’re proud to finally talk about the extraordinary work behind this missile and how we’re working with the U.S. government to rapidly scale production.”

Lockheed has been developing JATM for the U.S. Air Force and Navy to outrange and eventually replace the AIM-120 AMRAAM.

The company said the AIM-260 offers greater range and effectiveness than current U.S. air-to-air weapons. Public estimates put its range at more than 120 miles, a response to longer-range Chinese weapons such as the PL-15 .

Sized to fit the internal bays of fifth-generation fighters like the F-22 and F-35, the missile must deliver that added range with a footprint no larger than the AMRAAM it replaces.

The first public images of the missile were taken May 13, when aviation photographer Jonathan Tweedy photographed an AIM-260 loaded on a Navy F/A-18F Super Hornet at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida. The Aviationist published the photo two days later.

Lockheed also tied the framework to foreign military sales . Australia announced Aug. 6 it would invest about $520 million USD, or $736 million AU, to buy JATM for the Royal Australian Air Force , becoming the missile’s first export customer. The service plans to integrate it first on F/A-18F Super Hornets, then on F-35A Lightning IIs and EA-18G Growlers.

That order represents a fraction of what the U.S. has authorized. In March, it approved a potential sale to Australia of up to 450 missiles and associated test articles valued at $3.16 billion.

While some earlier 2026 framework deals with Lockheed came with public production targets, Thursday’s releases gave no JATM production rate or dollar value.

Michael Scanlon is a defense journalist covering air and space warfare. A former U.S. Air Force A-10 crew chief, he has supported land and sea programs for the U.S. Army, Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard.

items.title: US Air Force renews efforts to ensure units have accurate spouse contact information
items.author: Patricia Kime
items.summary: The Air Force is distributing cards instructing commanders on how to collect and download spouses' contact information to ensure family readiness.
items.body:
Pentagon

US Air Force renews efforts to ensure units have accurate spouse contact information

Cindy Wilsbach, right, the wife of Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Ken Wilsbach, left, speaks Sept. 16, 2026, at the Air & Space Forces Association's annual Air, Space & Cyber Conference. (Jud McCrehin/Air & Space Forces Association)

It’s been a problem as long as the existence of modern communications: Despite the need for commands to have accurate contact information for military spouses, some service members, military wives or husbands simply don’t want to be reached.

The failure of troops to provide phone numbers for spouses in the Air Force Personnel Accountability and Assessment System, however, can carry dire consequences. Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Scheiss recalled an incident in which he and his wife, Debbie, needed to reach a spouse whose husband had died in Syria.

But when they called the number on file, the phone simply rang and rang. It was the number for the airman’s cell phone.

“The number we were calling [was wrong] because he didn’t want his wife’s number to be on something,” Scheiss said during a forum on military families at the Air & Space Forces Association annual conference in Oxon Hill, Maryland, on Wednesday. “We are the most connected people in the world … but when the time is needed to contact people … don’t take away that ability for a spouse to be connected.”

The Air Force is launching an effort to improve the service’s ability to collect accurate contact information for spouses and provide it to units’ Key Support Program, the Air Force’s volunteer portion of a command’s family readiness efforts similar to Navy ombudsmen or Marine Corps family readiness volunteers.

Key Support Liaisons facilitate communications between commands and families — and often serve as the social foundation for military families when units are deployed.

Volunteers are required to keep phone numbers and other personal information confidential under the Privacy Act, but the unit phone trees they are provided are only as good as the information in AFPAAS, explained Cindy Wilsbach, wife of Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach.

“We’ve asked them to do this and [Key Support Liaisons] have stood up and said they will, yet we haven’t equipped them by giving them the contact information for our families,” Cindy Wilsbach said.

“When this thing kicked off in February,” she said, referring to the Iran war, “I heard from people around the globe … ‘Cindy, their spouse is gone, and this spouse has heard from no one. No one has contacted her, no one has reached out to her.’ It wasn’t just one or two people. I heard it from a lot of people.”

The service has started distributing cards to unit leaders that explain how leaders — most likely unit first sergeants — can pull unit personnel lists from AFPAAS and provide a comprehensive recall roster to their Key Support Liaison.

The four-step effort involves identifying the need, collecting the contact information, maintaining a roster and providing it to the liaison on a regular basis.

Collecting and distributing accurate information on family contacts may sound simple, but it’s been a problem “for a very long time,” Cindy Wilsbach said.

“We’ve heard it at every single base we’ve visited … so we’re hoping, with Legal’s blessing, that this is the way forward, that we will arm KSLs with the power to actually do what we’ve asked them to do,” she said.

Connection with the command, as well as one another, is a cornerstone of readiness, Cindy Wilsbach added. She said the liaisons are a vital resource for making initial contact with new families, sustaining families when units are deployed and providing support in emergencies.

The senior leaders and their spouses urged personnel attending the conference to keep their spouses’ contact information updated in AFPAAS, with Chief Master Sergeant of the Space Force John Bentivegna saying it’s the responsibility of leadership to make sure that spouses feel included.

“How many spouses … are maybe just waiting for someone to reach out to them. The worst that could happen is you send a note or make a phone call, send a text or an email, and you don’t get an answer back … but this is where leadership comes in — you got in there, and you got to take care,” Bentivegna said.

Patricia Kime is a senior writer covering military and veterans health care, medicine and personnel issues.

items.title: US Navy awards defense startup $200 million for Blackbeard hypersonic missile
items.author: Claire Barrett
items.summary: The U.S. Navy awarded defense startup Castelion $200 million for the production of its Blackbeard hypersonic missile.
items.body:
MilTech

US Navy awards defense startup $200 million for Blackbeard hypersonic missile

The Blackbeard hypersonic missile is a low-cost, scalable weapon that can be fielded across carrier strike groups. (Castelion)

The U.S. Navy awarded defense startup Castelion $200 million for the production of its Blackbeard hypersonic missile, a low-cost, scalable weapon that can be fielded across carrier strike groups, the service announced Tuesday .

The Navy championed the contract as one of the first successful examples of the Department of the Navy Rapid Capabilities Office and how it “has adapted its acquisition structure to more rapidly meet the needs of the warfighter. … By leveraging advanced commercial manufacturing methods and a vertically integrated production line, this landmark program introduces immediate ‘affordable mass’ to the fleet.”

Blackbeard is “an air-launched, hypersonic strike weapon that provides carrier-based strike fighters with a responsive, long-range, high-speed strike option against maritime and land targets, enhancing survivability against advanced air defenses while significantly increasing magazine depth,” the release notes.

The missile, according to Inside Defense , is intended to serve as a standoff weapon with a 200-nautical-mile range, arming aircraft including the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter and the F/A-18/E/F Super Hornet.

The Navy has long sought an air-launched hypersonic anti-surface missile and, since 2021, has pursued an air-breathing hypersonic cruise missile through the program dubbed Hypersonic Air-Launched Offensive Anti-Surface Warfare, or HALO, according to earlier reporting from The War Zone.

In subsequent years, Raytheon and Lockheed Martin competed for the contract, with the Navy hoping to field HALO before 2030. However, the service scrapped the program in 2024, citing budgetary constraints.

Castelion is now offering the Navy a low-cost solution to its current gap in its weapons systems.

In February, the Navy awarded the defense startup nearly $50 million after it selected Blackbeard for its Multimission Affordable Capacity Effector (MACE) program. The Navy earmarked $156 million in its fiscal 2027 budget request to procure 353 MACE missiles. And in June, the Navy awarded the company $23.4 million for pre-production prototypes and 50 associated storage and shipping containers, according to Castelion.

The latest contract awarded to Castelion leverages the Small Business Innovation Development Act from the 2026 National Defense Authorization Act “to rapidly transition successful technology developed through private capital investment directly into production. This approach reduces millions of dollars in redundant, non-recurring engineering costs while introducing aggressive commercial competition into the munitions production ecosystem,” according to the release.

And with Castelion’s emphasis on low cost and producibility for Blackbeard, the Navy is seemingly positioning itself well in the post-HALO hypersonic missile world.

Claire Barrett is an editor and military history correspondent for Military Times. She is also a World War II researcher with an unparalleled affinity for Sir Winston Churchill and Michigan football.

PDF , 131 KB , 4 pages

Details

In line with the government’s transparency and open data initiative, the Military Court Service is to publish the court listings for the military court centres.

Each court listing covers the next one or two week assize period. This will be published on the internet by the last working day in advance of the assize period.

In addition to this, the court listings are published using digital signage technology within the reception areas of both military court centres.

Please be aware that the court listings are subject to change after publication, if you wish to find out more please contact the relevant military court centre. Details can be found at the bottom of each court listing.

items.title: UK must focus on the Atlantic, ‘foundation’ of Britain’s security: Navy chief
items.author: Rudy Ruitenberg
items.summary: The Royal Navy is spending a growing amount of time and resources to monitor Russian vessels, on average devoting two British warships every week to it.
items.body:
Europe

UK must focus on the Atlantic, ‘foundation’ of Britain’s security: Navy chief

Crew members wave goodbye to family and friends as air-defense destroyer HMS Dragon sets sail from Portsmouth Harbour on March 10, 2026, in Portsmouth, England. (Leon Neal/Getty Images)

PARIS – The United Kingdom must strengthen naval readiness to keep the Atlantic open and protect the sea lanes, undersea cables and energy infrastructure vital to the country, the chief of the Royal Navy said.

Britain faces threats not seen since the Cold War, with Russia increasingly probing the North Atlantic and around critical underwater infrastructure, First Sea Lord Gen. Gwyn Jenkins said in a speech at the historical Admiralty House in central London on Wednesday, with repeated references to the Battle for the Atlantic during World War II.

Jenkins cited the memoirs of Winston Churchill on the significance of the Atlantic, saying the wartime leader understood the sea is not peripheral to Britain but existential. The Atlantic remains central to U.K. security and to NATO’s ability to reinforce Europe, according to the First Sea Lord , who said a “whole-nation effort” is required to defend the sea.

RELATED

NATO allies foil Russian subsea cable sabotage plot

The clandestine Russian operation was carried out by Moscow’s GUGI undersea warfare directorate to test a destructive sabotage capability, sources said.

“We must know what is happening in the Atlantic, protect what matters, keep open the sea lanes, and convince any adversary that the cost of coercion or aggression would outweigh any possible gain,” Jenkins said, according to a transcript of the speech. “If we are to prevail in the Atlantic again, we must strengthen our warfighting readiness and rediscover what it means to be a maritime nation.”

The First Sea Lord said British dependence on the Atlantic has grown in the past 80 years, with almost all of the U.K.’s trade moving by sea, and almost all its energy, food, raw materials and exports flowing via maritime routes. He noted a “dangerous paradox,” saying that while the Atlantic has arguably never mattered more to the country, the sea is increasingly invisible in the public’s mind.

Control of the Atlantic has always been closely linked to control of its northern approaches, the Navy chief said, citing the defeat of Norway during World War II that allowed the Nazis to threaten allied shipping lanes, and the importance of the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap during the Cold War.

The Norwegian Sea, the Arctic and the northern approaches are not distant theaters but “form our open sea border with Russia,” according to Jenkins, who said the Joint Expeditionary Force is increasingly important there. The U.K.-led military alliance includes the five Nordic countries, the three Baltic states as well as the Netherlands.

Jenkins said the ten JEF countries will finalize a “Northern Navies” agreement this year to move beyond what he called episodic activity and to create a persistent, integrated maritime force, in response to the security threat presented by Russia.

Russia has advanced submarines that are increasingly difficult to track, long-range precision weapons and specialist deep-water systems, and is “probing, testing and mapping,” Jenkins said. The Royal Navy is spending a growing amount of time and resources to monitor Russian vessels, on average deploying two British warships every week for that purpose, according to the navy chief.

The First Sea Lord defended plans to create a “hybrid Navy,” saying future advantage will come from integrated networks linking crewed vessels, drones, sensors and data. He said that while there are skeptics, the concept is not optional.

“It is no longer possible to defend a vast, contested ocean with crewed warships alone,” Jenkins said. “A ship operating alone is now vulnerable. But a ship commanding a network of large uncrewed escorts, drones and autonomous sensors, that is a different proposition. That’s why we must blend old and new, crewed and uncrewed.”

Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

Preserving Jobs and Tax Revenue in the Age of AI: Q&A with Carter Price

Commentary

Sep 17, 2026

If AI starts to replace jobs, it isn't just American workers who will feel the loss of income. So will the U.S. Treasury.

Nearly two-thirds of all federal revenue comes from taxes levied on human labor, a recent RAND study noted. That revenue will not be easy to make up if AI starts to put large numbers of people out of work.

Carter Price has been looking for ways to rebalance the tax code so that it doesn't incentivize employers to replace humans with AI. He's a mathematician at RAND and co-director of the RAND Von Furstenberg Family Budget Model Initiative . And he has an idea for how to give workers an edge in the age of AI.

How does the existing tax code disincentivize keeping human workers on the job?

We went through all 7,000 pages of the tax code with a tool we built as part of the RAND Budget Model Initiative. It allows us to identify every provision, every line item, and its implications. There's a lot in there. But we identified several places where the existing U.S tax code works against companies hiring or keeping workers.

The employer payroll tax is one obvious example. Companies have to pay that tax for every worker they hire, so more workers means more expense. Meanwhile, the tax code allows companies to write off the depreciation of big, expensive assets early, before those assets actually wear out. That can make buying something like a robotic system much more cost-effective—which makes that tax write-off a direct subsidy for displacing human workers.

What's your idea to change the incentives here?

You and I pay progressive taxes on our income. That means if we make more money, we move into a higher tax bracket.

Our idea is somewhat similar, but for companies. The government would tax high corporate profits per worker in addition to taxing their income overall.

Imagine a company makes $1 million in profit and has 100 employees. Its profit per worker is $10,000. Now let's say that company brings in a lot of AI and lays off all but ten of its workers. Now its profit per worker is $100,000, and it just moved into a higher tax bracket. It's going to pay more in taxes for that same $1 million in profit.

AI might still be so much more efficient that it still makes sense for some companies to replace those workers. This tax structure wouldn't stand in the way of that.

But where the current tax code sometimes disincentivizes keeping human workers, our proposed change would flip the script. It would put the tax code more on the side of workers instead of on the side of AI and automation.

What else did your tax code analysis find that could help promote employment?

We found a lot of special, niche provisions that are just scattered throughout the tax code. You could eliminate those and really clean everything up. There are three different clean-energy vehicle tax provisions, for example, and they all do pretty much the same thing.

These niche provisions pointed us to a suite of changes that could really make a difference. The government could eliminate those special tax breaks. That would bring in additional revenue.

The federal government could then eliminate the employer payroll tax and replace it with two business taxes: one a flat tax on business revenue, and the other the per-worker tax on high profits.

Companies would be no worse off. The government would balance the loss of revenue from eliminating the payroll tax with an increase from eliminating special tax carve-outs. And we'd be incentivizing human employment instead of using tax breaks to incentivize things like investments in distilled spirits.

Our proposed change would put the tax code more on the side of workers instead of on the side of AI and automation.

What would it take to implement those changes?

It takes an act of Congress to change the Internal Revenue Code. But that's a low barrier compared to what some other popular policy ideas that are floating around would face. For example, a value-added tax, which would be like a nationwide sales tax, would require an entirely new tax-collection infrastructure. And a federal wealth tax, which could generate revenue from huge concentrations of wealth, would require a constitutional amendment in addition to new tax-collection infrastructure.

By contrast, policymakers could at least theoretically wake up tomorrow and pass a law that would make the tax code more robust by reducing its dependence on income from labor.

Furthermore, simplifying the tax code would give people back millions of hours that they currently spend filling out forms. It would improve the efficiency of the economy, and that's something everyone can like.

What motivates you to do this work?

I'm a mathematician. And there have been a lot of headlines about the advances that AI models have made in mathematics in particular. AI can generate code that would take a human hours, or even days, to write. I'm biased, but I think human mathematicians still provide a lot of value that AI can't fully replace. I'm not sure that will be true forever. But until that changes, we shouldn't rush into replacing workers with AI, and our tax code certainly shouldn't incentivize employers to do so.

PDF , 17.4 KB , 1 page

Details

Related information

The regulated community should use the MAA request for change ( RFC ) form to submit a proposal for change to regulatory articles ( RA ’s) or associated manuals.

To request clarification of regulation meaning, routine correspondence methods such as email, letter and telephone may be used.

The MAA may still request a completed MAA RFC form, depending on the nature of the enquiry.

Notwithstanding that formal amendment may result from a clarification request, initial requests for clarification should not be submitted on a MAA RFC form.

The MAA RFC form can be submitted via email to the MAA regulatory publications team ( MRPT ) at dsa-maa-mrp enquires . If clarification is required regarding the need for submission of an MAA RFC form, then the regulated community can contact the MRPT .

items.title: Germany sending fighter jets to Latvia to protect election from drone incidents
items.author: Linus Höller
items.summary: Germany will send four Eurofighter jets to defend Latvian airspace during upcoming elections, amid concerns over drone incursions from Russia and Belarus.
items.body:
Europe

Germany sending fighter jets to Latvia to protect election from drone incidents

An Eurofighter aircraft of the German Air Force sits on the tarmac at the Latvian air base of Lielvarde in April 2024. (Alexander Welscher/picture alliance via Getty Images)

VIENNA — Germany will send four Eurofighter jets to defend Latvian airspace during its upcoming elections, as concerns over drone incursions from neighboring Russia and Belarus remain high.

Berlin plans to dispatch four Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets, alongside a contingent of several dozen soldiers and technicians, to the Lielvārde air base in central Latvia. They will be there for a week in late September and early October, the German ministry of defense said in a statement.

Latvian authorities had requested support from allies to secure the skies over the country during the general election, Germany said. The Latvian parliamentary election is scheduled to take place Oct. 3.

The mission is billed as part of NATO’s enhanced air policing north, or eAPN, in the Baltic States, though the short, one-week timeline and narrower election focus set it apart from the alliance’s routine four-month rotations.

None of the three small Baltic States possess their own fighter aircraft. Unlike northern Estonia and southern Lithuania, Latvia is not usually home to permanently stationed NATO jets; instead, the allied aircraft stationed in the neighboring states also cover Latvian skies.

The Baltic states in particular have been calling for strong NATO commitments to secure the alliance’s eastern flank, as governments in the three small countries feel particularly threatened by Russia. This year, repeated unauthorized drone incursions have additionally put the countries on edge. Some of these have been identified as Ukrainian drones that strayed off course from their targets in Russia, while other instances remain unidentified.

Significantly, Italian NATO jets in neighboring Lithuania shot down a suspected Russian-made drone this week after it crossed the border from Belarus. It was the first time a drone was shot down in Lithuanian airspace.

Lielvārde air base, where the German Eurofighters will be stationed during their mission, has also seen rotating contingents of other NATO countries’ fighter jets. Just a few weeks ago, in late August, two Turkish F-16 fighter jets visited the base. In April, French Rafale jets based out of Šiauliai, Lithuania, visited the airfield. NATO has also used the base for its AWACS aircraft during missions along the Russian border.

Latvia and its two Baltic neighbors have been members of NATO since 2004, joining alongside fellow eastern flank countries Slovakia, Romania and Bulgaria, and Slovenia.

Linus Höller is Defense News' Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish.

items.title: India says China has scaled back troop numbers along their border
items.author: Anjana Pasricha
items.summary: Both countries had amassed tens of thousands of troops along their poorly demarcated Himalayan border following a deadly clash in 2020.
items.body:
Asia Pacific

India says China has scaled back troop numbers along their border

This video frame grab taken from footage recorded in mid-June 2020 and released by China Central Television (CCTV) on Feb. 20, 2021, shows Indian soldiers crossing a river during an incident where Chinese and Indian troops clashed in the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in the Galwan Valley, in the Karakoram Mountains in the Himalayas. (CCTV/AFP via Getty Images)

NEW DELHI — India’s Defense Ministry said that China significantly reduced troop deployment along the border with India in 2025 as increased political, diplomatic and military engagement helped ease tensions between the two Asian powers.

Both countries had amassed tens of thousands of troops along their poorly demarcated Himalayan border following a deadly clash in 2020.

“The year 2025 witnessed significant reduction in deployment of People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Force opposite Northern Borders, with 10 Combined Arms Brigade size forces each deployed in areas along the LAC and in traditional training areas,” the Defense Ministry stated in its annual report for 2025-26 released Monday.

The LAC or Line of Actual Control refers to the roughly 3,500 kilometers long Indo-Chinese frontier in the Himalayas. Much of the boundary remains disputed.

The report said that bilateral interactions at political, diplomatic and military levels had facilitated “positive developments along the northern border, leading to stability.”

However the Defense Ministry did not provide figures for Indian troop deployments along the Indo-Chinese border but said that the Indian Army’s deployment “in all sectors” along the LAC remained “robust, well poised, and prepared to deal with any emerging contingency.”

The report also highlighted India’s accelerated construction of tunnels, roads and other all-weather infrastructure in the Himalayas, which it said is critical for the rapid movement of troops, equipment and supplies.

Analysts point out that China has similarly expanded infrastructure on its side of the border in recent years, suggesting that even as troop deployment eases, long-term military readiness remains a priority for both sides along their border.

“Maintaining a strong dissuasive posture and preparedness along the borders is an imperative. We cannot scale down our defenses irrespective of troop numbers,” said retired Brigadier Arun Sahgal, who directs the Forum for Strategic Initiatives in New Delhi.

The report comes amid a broader thaw in India-China relations. Chinese President Xi Jinping visited New Delhi for the annual BRICS summit last week, his first trip to India in seven years. The visit marked another step in efforts by the two countries to stabilize relations after years of tensions triggered by the 2020 border clash.

After a meeting between the two leaders on the sidelines of the summit, Xi said China viewed India-China relations from a “strategic and long-term perspective” and called on the two countries to support one another and pursue common development. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said peace and tranquility along the disputed border were essential to the continued development of bilateral ties.

India’s foreign ministry said that “the two leaders expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question.”

Tensions between India and China began to ease after Xi and Modi met in Russia in October 2024 leading to an agreement that helped end the military standoff in eastern Ladakh.
