items.title: Guidance: Spousal employment - Supplementary Agreement Germany
items.summary: The NATO Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) and the Supplementary Agreement are the international legal agreements that enable UK Defence to operate in Germany.
items.body:
The NATO SOFA is a multinational agreement between nations enabling the operation of a nation’s defence task in the territory of another nation.

In Germany, the stationing and operation of UK Defence personnel is governed by the Supplementary Agreement to the NATO SOFA. The Supplementary Agreement expands upon the provisions of the NATO SOFA and forms part of German domestic law, providing the detailed legal framework under which UK Defence operates in Germany.

Overview

Neither the NATO SOFA nor the Supplementary Agreement provides a direct legal entitlement for accompanying spouses or family members to undertake employment in Germany.

The agreements provide a basis for lawful residence and status in Germany for eligible dependants accompanying members of the force or civilian component. Any employment activity undertaken by a dependant must, however, comply with applicable German law.

The UK Ministry of Defence cannot grant authority, permission, or exemptions allowing spouses or dependants to work in Germany. Responsibility for ensuring compliance with host nation legislation rests with the individual and, where applicable, their employer.

There are several routes through which accompanying spouses may lawfully undertake employment within Germany, subject to the relevant legal and regulatory requirements.

Employment within the German Economy

The status of an accompanying spouse is recognised under German immigration arrangements associated with the Supplementary Agreement and NATO SOFA framework. Consequently, accompanying spouses generally do not require a separate residence permit or work permit to seek employment in the German economy.

Individuals employed by German or other locally established employers will be subject to German legislation and jurisdiction. This may include:

employment law

taxation requirements

social security contributions

health insurance obligations

pension arrangements

other statutory and regulatory requirements

The decision to undertake employment within the German economy is a personal one. Individuals are responsible for ensuring that their employment arrangements comply fully with German law.

Neither the Supplementary Agreement nor the NATO SOFA provides exemptions from German employment, tax, social security, healthcare, or other legal obligations arising from employment.

Operating a Business or Undertaking Self-Employment in Germany

Accompanying spouses may be able to establish and operate a business, trade, profession, or other self-employed activity within the Federal Republic of Germany, subject to the relevant approvals, registrations, and regulatory requirements imposed by the German authorities.

Any business activity undertaken for commercial gain and participating in the German economy will ordinarily be subject to applicable German legislation. This may include taxation, social security obligations, health insurance requirements, licensing provisions, and other regulatory controls.

Individuals considering self-employment or the operation of a business should seek appropriate professional advice from qualified German legal, tax, and financial advisers before commencing any activity.

Care should be taken to maintain a clear distinction between any commercial activity and the rights, privileges, or status derived from dependant status under the NATO SOFA and Supplementary Agreement.

International remote working (IRW)

Neither the NATO SOFA nor the Supplementary Agreement establishes a legal framework for International Remote Working (IRW).

Remote working arrangements are a matter between the employee and their employer. The UK MOD cannot authorise or validate remote working arrangements undertaken within the territory of another sovereign state. This includes those attracting the term Crown Servant (Civil or Military) not assigned to Germany for the purpose of their employment.

Before commencing any form of remote working from Germany, both the employee and employer should satisfy themselves that the arrangement is lawful and compliant with all relevant German legal requirements.

Consideration should be given to matters including:

employment legislation

taxation obligations

social security requirements

healthcare obligations

health and safety legislation

data protection and privacy regulations

any other relevant regulatory requirements

Depending on the circumstances, German law may impose obligations on either the employee or employer, even where the employer is established outside Germany and the work is undertaken remotely.

Employees and employers are strongly encouraged to seek independent legal and professional advice from appropriately qualified German advisers before commencing any remote working arrangement.

Where the work involves access to official, government, or sensitive information, additional security considerations may apply. Individuals should ensure compliance with all relevant departmental security policies and seek advice from their employing organisation where necessary.

Key Principles

The Supplementary Agreement and NATO SOFA do not provide a right to employment for accompanying spouses.

Any employment, self-employment, or business activity in Germany must comply with German law.

The MOD cannot grant permission or exemptions for employment activities in Germany.

International Remote Working is not covered by the Supplementary Agreement or NATO SOFA.

Individuals and employers are responsible for ensuring that any employment arrangement is lawful and compliant with applicable host nation requirements.

items.title: Japanese Global Hawk drone splashes down in crash
items.author: Gordon Arthur
items.summary: A Japanese Global Hawk drone nosedived into the Sea of Japan this week, instantly slashing the country’s fleet of these drones by a third.
items.body:
Asia Pacific

Japanese Global Hawk drone splashes down in crash

This picture taken on Jan. 23, 2023, shows a Global Hawk unmanned surveillance aircraft of the Japan Air Self-Defence Force (JASDF) in Misawa, Aomori prefecture. (Jiji Press / AFP via Getty Images)

CHRISTCHURCH, New Zealand — A Japanese Global Hawk drone nosedived into the Sea of Japan on Sept. 15, instantly slashing the country’s fleet of these large-wingspan, unmanned surveillance aircraft by a third.

Japan paid roughly $163 million for Northrop Grumman to manufacture each of its three RQ-4B Block 30i Global Hawks nearly a decade ago.

The Japan Air Self-Defense Force (JASDF) on Sept. 16 revealed that it lost contact with the high-altitude drone at 12:55 p.m., before losing its radar signature three minutes later over international waters.

The JASDF’s 502nd Squadron operates its Global Hawks from Misawa Air Base in northern Japan. Before crashing, the drone had taken off at 10.20 a.m. on an unspecified mission, with JASDF Chief of Staff Gen. Takehiro Morita only divulging, “This particular flight was not a training exercise.”

One mission for Japanese Global Hawks, which can stay aloft for 32 hours at altitudes of up to 60,000 ft, is monitoring North Korean missile launch preparations. They are also useful for keeping an eye on Chinese military activities.

Morita said a Japan Coast Guard helicopter spotted debris in the water just 50 minutes after it had lost contact. Other assets spotted further wreckage and took photos, enabling precise identification of the aircraft.

No cause of the accident was revealed.

Japan received its first Global Hawk in March 2022, with the other two arriving later that year. Their integrated payload contains an electro-optic/infrared sensor, synthetic aperture radar and ground moving target indicator.

The Global Hawk purchase was controversial in Japan given their enormous cost and the fact that the U.S. retained tight control over the aircraft’s technology and the processing of gathered data.

Global Hawks possess the longest reach of any Japanese drone, so the loss of one among such a small fleet will be sorely missed.

However, as Japan increasingly prioritizes unmanned technologies, the Japan Maritime Self Defense Force is planning to induct the first of 23 MQ-9B SeaGuardians in 2027. Although these drones have a shorter endurance and range than the Global Hawk, Tokyo will use them for maritime domain awareness.

Japan’s draft 2027 defense budget requested US$1.88 billion for the first 17 SeaGuardians. These will take over some of the missions currently performed by P-1 and older P-3C Orion maritime patrol aircraft.

Incidentally, the U.S. Air Force currently has three RQ-4B Global Hawks stationed at Yokota Air Base in Tokyo, after relocating them from Guam in May to avoid the typhoon season.

The United States planned to quickly retire all its Global Hawks, but it will now keep operating them until 2033. After that, there will be only three in South Korea and two in Japan still flying.

Gordon Arthur is an Asia correspondent for Defense News. After a 20-year stint working in Hong Kong, he now resides in New Zealand. He has attended military exercises and defense exhibitions in about 20 countries around the Asia-Pacific region.

The Germany Enabling Office (GEO) is the United Kingdom’s military mission in Germany and the responsible authority for enabling, monitoring and assuring the conduct of United Kingdom defence in Germany under the United Kingdom’s obligations to the NATO Status of Forces Agreement (NATO SOFA) and the Supplementary Agreement (SA) in Germany.

The NATO SOFA and the SA are the international legal agreements enabling the military of the United Kingdom to operate in Germany.

Our engagement with UK defence personnel in Germany, and where applicable broader Europe, is routinely through the customer-facing UK National Support Elements (UK NSE).

Though the GEO is not directly customer facing you will receive communication from us via your NSE. Our routine official communications with those NSE are in the form of information notes.

Where possible those information notes will be made available on this webpage.

items.title: Battle for the Atlantic
items.summary: First Sea Lord and Chief of the Naval Staff General Sir Gwyn Jenkins delivered a speech at Admiralty House, Department of Naval Research.
items.body:
Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen.

Thank you for joining us, and my thanks to the Department for Naval Research for organising today’s symposium.

As we gather here at Admiralty House, the importance of sea power will not be lost on any of you.

That is because our history has been shaped by the sea.

Because our prosperity, security and influence have for centuries depended on our ability to master it, protect what moves across it, and deny its advantages to those who threaten us.

That’s why my speech today is focused on the Atlantic.

Not simply as a vast body of water, or a theatre of past conflict, but as a foundation of Britain’s security.

Eighty years ago, Britain and her allies fought the longest campaign of the Second World War at sea.

It was fought by sailors, merchant seamen, aircrew, dockyard workers, engineers, scientists and codebreakers…

By men and women who kept Britain alive as Europe fell under Nazi occupation.

Convoys crossed a hostile ocean in atrocious weather, under air attack and constant U-boat threat.

They carried the food, fuel, raw materials, weapons and reinforcements on which our national survival depended.

In 1941, Churchill named this struggle the Battle of the Atlantic.

It was the prospect of losing this Battle – not the Blitz, not the threat to the Empire in the East – that truly frightened him.

As Churchill observed later in his memoirs, Britain’s ability to “carry on the war, or even keep ourselves alive,” rested fundamentally “on our mastery of the ocean routes and the free approach and entry to our ports.”

Churchill attached such significance to the Atlantic because he understood something important.

The sea is not peripheral to Britain – it is existential.

If those maritime arteries had been severed during the War…

Had Britain lost the Atlantic…

Our life support would have been switched off.

We would have struggled to cling on before the Americans joined the fight…

Europe would not have been liberated…

And victory would have been impossible.

That does not diminish the role of our other services, whose contribution to the war was also vital.

Yesterday, we marked the 86th anniversary of the Battle of Britain, a campaign that denied the Luftwaffe air superiority and was also integral to our survival.

And as the son of an RAF crypto mechanic, I know how important air power was and remains to our nation.

But the point I am making is this:

Without the Royal Navy and the RAF, who is to say whether Hitler would have abandoned Operation Sealion and switched his focus to invading Russia instead.

Who is to say whether the Army would have been able to campaign in North Africa, the Med or in mainland Europe.

Sea power not only sustained us during the War.

It arguably saved us.

Lose the war at sea and you lose the war.

That was the warning of Admiral Pound, the First Sea Lord of the day – and it remains true now.

If we are to prevail in the Atlantic again, we must strengthen our warfighting readiness and rediscover what it means to be a maritime nation.

Not because history repeats itself perfectly.

It doesn’t.

But because the factors that made the Atlantic decisive eighty years ago remain decisive today.

The world may have changed beyond recognition – but our dependence on the Atlantic has only grown since.

Almost all our trade moves by sea, and America remains by far our biggest trading partner.

Almost all our energy, food, raw materials and exports flow through maritime routes.

Beneath the waves, our nuclear deterrent protects the nation.

Undersea cables carry almost all data, transactions, and communications on which modern life depends.

In all these areas, the Atlantic is critical.

During the war, the British people understood that a submarine attack on an allied convoy hundreds of miles away had direct consequences at home.

But today, we have reached a dangerous paradox…

The sea, the Atlantic, has arguably never mattered more to Britain.

We are certainly much more reliant on it than we were in the 1930s.

And yet it has become increasingly invisible in the public’s mind.

Supermarket shelves are filled, homes are heated, money moves instantly and the internet turbocharges our modern lives.

We have made this huge progress seem effortless.

But it was not effortless.

It was earned. It was fought for. We have continuously defended it.

And if that defence fails, the consequences will be felt quickly in every household, every business and every department of state.

Our adversaries understand that.

They understand our dependence on the sea and the seabed.

They understand that the Atlantic is not empty space.

It is strategic terrain: the bridge between North America, Europe and with the world.

The route through which NATO reinforcement would move.

The space through which our trade, energy, data and deterrence are sustained.

That is why the lessons of the War remain so important.

In the 1940s, the question was whether Britain could stay connected to the industrial, economic and military strength of North America and its Empire.

Today, in an age of missiles, cyber, space surveillance, and rapid technological change, we also face added challenges, because the seabed has become a new arena of contest.

Uncrewed systems are changing how we fight, advancing at a rate many nations are struggling to keep pace with.

Information is moving faster than it has ever moved before.

And yet, many of the fundamentals remain the same.

The Atlantic is the same body of water…

We are still an island…

We still rely on it to move the goods, fuel and commodities we rely on…

And our most important alliances are still trans-Atlantic.

That is why this issue reaches beyond uniform.

The Atlantic is a military, industrial, diplomatic and economic challenge – and an opportunity.

That is why we need a whole-nation effort if we are to continue to defend it.

History shows us this.

The original Battle of the Atlantic was not won by one decisive action.

It was won by cumulative advantage: better intelligence, faster shipbuilding, improved tactics, effective air cover, convoy discipline and a willingness to learn under pressure.

It was won by leadership, the spirit to fight and the urge to win.

The same approach is required today, but with different tools and in a different context.

We should not allow the complexity of modern technology to muddy what is a simple task.

We must know what is happening in the Atlantic, protect what matters, keep open the sea lanes, and convince any adversary that the cost of coercion or aggression would outweigh any possible gain.

That is the test of warfighting readiness.

Can we fight tonight? Can we sustain the fight tomorrow? And can we adapt faster than our adversaries?

That is the standard by which the Navy must be judged.

The Battle of the Atlantic demonstrated another enduring lesson.

There is only one thing worse than fighting with allies, and that is fighting without them.

No nation secured the Atlantic alone in the 1940s, and no nation will do so now.

Victory depended on Allied integration: navies, merchant fleets, air forces, intelligence, scientists and industry working to a common purpose.

That same principle underpins NATO today.

In any major crisis, NATO’s ability to reinforce Europe depends upon secure access across the Atlantic.

It remains central to collective defence.

That is why the Royal Navy’s role in the Atlantic cannot be separated from NATO’s wider mission.

Our task is to contribute to collective deterrence, support the movement of Allied forces, protect critical infrastructure, maintain awareness and ensure freedom of manoeuvre.

This is also why partnerships matter.

Whether through NATO, bilateral relationships or the Joint Expeditionary Force, our security is strengthened when we operate alongside allies who share our interests and values.

For the United Kingdom, this is both a responsibility and an opportunity.

We are a nuclear power, a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, a founding member of NATO and the framework nation for the JEF.

We are still one of the most powerful navies in the world.

Our geography, history and alliances give us both a particular stake in the North Atlantic and the ability to act with others at scale.

Which leads me onto the third lesson of the War: our northern flank matters.

The Atlantic cannot be understood without understanding the High North, because control of the ocean has always been closely linked to control of its northern approaches.

The consequences of losing control were painfully evident in 1940, when Norway’s defeat gave the Nazis control of the coastline and deep-water fjords from which they were able to threaten allied shipping lanes in the Atlantic.

Later, the Greenland-Iceland-UK Gap became integral in the Cold War.

And today, its relevance remains undiminished.

The Norwegian Sea, the Arctic and the northern approaches are not distant theatres.

They are the gateway to our backyard; they form our open sea border with Russia.

They are where British security, NATO and European stability come together.

And it is also where the JEF makes an increasingly important contribution.

For more than a decade, the UK has led ten like-minded nations that are able to respond quickly to threats in the High North, North Atlantic and Baltic.

It complements NATO, but it also gives us the speed, political alignment and geographic focus to seize the initiative early.

As First Sea Lord, I have been determined to make that partnership stronger.

That is why we have been working with the JEF members on a new Northern Navies agreement, which we will finalise this year.

It will move us beyond episodic activity to a persistent, integrated maritime force.

Navies that train together, exercise together, plan together and, if necessary, fight together.

It requires common systems, shared digital networks, common doctrine, shared logistics and stockpiles…

This isn’t just about fighting together. It’s about building a common British and Norwegian frigate force.

It’s about ensuring a Danish frigate can seamlessly takeover from a British warship in the Atlantic, while also taking control of our flotilla of uncrewed ships and sensors that will remain in position for months on end.

This is how we turn collective strength into credible deterrence.

This is how we create a Vanguard for NATO.

A family of Northern Navies, led by the UK, stronger than the sum of its parts.

Making the Hybrid Navy real, with allies.

The reason why we need this is simple: the greatest threat to our security today is Russia.

That threat is felt most acutely in the maritime domain – in the North Atlantic, in the High North.

Russia retains advanced submarines that are increasingly difficult to track, long-range precision weapons, and specialist systems designed to operate deep underwater.

It is increasingly active in our domain, and we are spending increasing amounts of time and resource monitoring Russian vessels and the shadow fleet.

On average, two Royal Navy warships are now being deployed every week for this purpose.

Russia is probing, testing, and mapping.

It seeks advantage in the grey zone, particularly around the critical undersea infrastructure on which modern societies rely.

And among Ukraine’s western allies, Russia considers us to be one of its greatest foes.

We know that Russia is probing us for weakness.

And we are facing threats…in a way we have not been since the Cold War.

That does not mean we are returning to the days before the Berlin Wall fell.

Nor am I saying that war is inevitable. There are strong parallels, but this is not the 1930s.

The circumstances are different, the technologies have changed, and the context is more complex.

But many of the underlying challenges remain.

That is why the Royal Navy continues to invest in anti-submarine warfare, underwater surveillance, maritime aviation and Allied integration.

This is why we are building the Hybrid Navy.

This is not about seeking confrontation.

It is about preventing it through credible capability, strong alliances, presence and the ability to respond immediately when required.

During the Second World War, German U-boats sought to isolate Britain by attacking the merchant shipping.

Today, the form of the threat is different, but the significance of the underwater domain has grown rather than diminished.

Critical undersea infrastructure is now part of the strategic landscape. Cables, pipelines, sensors and energy networks connect nations, markets and command systems.

They are difficult to monitor, hard to repair at speed and increasingly integral to national resilience.

The day that the UK declared war on Germany, the allies severed its transatlantic telegraph cables.

I pray it does not happen, but were we to go to war again, we know our enemies will try to use the same playbook against us.

That is why protection of the High North, the Atlantic, and of our underwater CNI is not just about naval capability.

It also rests on intelligence, industry, law enforcement, commercial partnerships and close allied coordination.

It is a national endeavour.

The Royal Marines Commandos also play a crucial role in that effort.

The Atlantic campaign was never fought at sea alone.

Its outcome depended upon control of key geography around the wider Atlantic basin, and that lesson remains directly relevant to the northern flank today.

The ability to monitor, secure and influence activity across the maritime domain requires more than ships and submarines.

It requires forces able to operate where sea and land intersect, to work with allies in difficult terrain, and to create advantage before a crisis becomes a conflict.

That is where the Commandos make a uniquely important contribution.

Tough, resilient and resourceful, honed for some of the toughest environments on the planet, they are the tip of the spear when it comes to NATO’s strike forces.

And it is through them that we help create conditions for maritime operations to succeed.

The strategic logic would be familiar to the Commandos of the Second World War.

In May 1940, the Royal Marines led the pre-emptive occupation of Iceland, denying Germany a potential Atlantic base and enabling Allied ships and aircraft to support the convoys.

At St Nazaire, in March 1942, Commandos destroyed the dry dock that could have supported Tirpitz and other German warships raiding those convoys.

And months later, Royal Marines paddled by night into occupied Bordeaux during Operation Frankton, damaging vital Axis shipping and disrupting the blockade runners that sustained Germany’s war effort.

Today, the Commando Force may have undergone a generational transformation – but it remains just as important to our success.

The Royal Marines are part of an integrated fighting system. They have also evolved over the past decade because modern warfare demands adaptation.

The more we integrate, the more we adapt, the greater our advantage over our adversaries.

That logic also sits at the heart of the most radical and far-reaching reform we are undertaking currently: the move to a Hybrid Navy.

The maritime battlespace is becoming increasingly distributed, connected and data-driven.

Our future advantage will come from integrated networks combining ships, submarines, aircraft, autonomous systems, sensors, data and people.

Ukraine has shown how quickly maritime warfare can change.

In the Black Sea, uncrewed systems and long-range strikes have destroyed a Russian fleet that once seemed dominant.

In the Gulf and the Red Sea, drones and missiles have shown how quickly global trade can be disrupted.

The lesson is not that traditional platforms no longer matter.

It is that it is no longer possible to defend a vast, contested ocean with crewed warships alone.

A ship operating alone is now vulnerable.

But a ship commanding a network of large uncrewed escorts, drones and autonomous sensors…that is a different proposition.

That’s why we must blend old and new. Crewed and uncrewed.

We need a connected fighting force.

This is about changing how we generate combat power.

It will make the Fleet bigger, more lethal, harder to target and knock out of the fight, while also allowing us to adapt faster and impose more dilemma on the enemy.

That is the Hybrid Navy in a nutshell.

Unsurprisingly, we are shaping it around the Atlantic…

Through our Atlantic Series…

Atlantic Bastion is about defending the UK’s continuous at sea deterrent and the critical national infrastructure on which our country, economy and allies depend.

It is the creation of a defensive net across the North Atlantic: crewed and uncrewed ships, drones, sensors, artificial intelligence and weapons working above, on and below the sea to detect, deter and, if necessary, neutralise hostile activity.

Atlantic Shield is about protecting the homeland, the Fleet and our allies from drones, hypersonic weapons and ballistic threats through modern air and missile defence.

And Atlantic Strike is about giving us the ability to hit harder, from greater distance, if an adversary attacks us.

These are the practical building blocks of a new way of fighting.

A new Atlantic Fleet.

The objective is clear: to create a force that can detect threats earlier, respond faster, strike more precisely, survive in the most contested conditions and integrate better with allies.

Yes it is radical, yes we are early adopters, and yes there are sceptics.

But let me be clear: the Hybrid Navy is not opional.

And nor is the need to change our relationship with industry.

During the War we did not just outfight Nazi Germany; we innovated faster and built ships and aircraft at a pace the Reich simply could not match.

The same must be true again now if we are to prevail.

That means we have to move at the speed of the threat.

Software can change a system overnight. Commercial technology can reach the battlefield in days. Our procurement, testing and adoption cycles must reflect that reality.

That means more experimentation, more courage to fail quickly, and the ability to scale what works.

Yes, that creates more risk.

But as First Sea Lord, the only risk that really keeps me up at night is being asked to go to war – and losing.

That is the one risk I will not accept – because my job is not to lose.

My job is to win.

So, as we look to the future, what more must we do?

First, we must not lose focus on the here and now.

We must keep the Atlantic open.

We must continue to protect shipping, reinforcement routes, subsea cables, energy infrastructure and the deterrent.

We are recapitalising the entire nuclear enterprise for the first time since its creation.

We are growing the fleet, with 13 new frigates..

Six command ships for the Hybrid Navy…

Fleet solid support ships…

Four amphibious transport ships for our Commandos…

Two new Astute-class boats, four new Dreadnought-class submarines, and up to 12 next generations SSNs.

We have a Defence Investment Plan, unlocking our uncrewed systems and the Atlantic Series.

But there are plenty of obstacles that risk slowing us down.

We must be relentless in identifying and removing them.

Second, we must invest in people.

Technology changes the character of warfare, but it does not win wars.

Our people remain decisive – and it is leadership, leadership excellence, that wins wars.

War will always remain a contest of human will. That is why we must equip our people with the skills and leadership tools to enable them to win at all levels.

They will have to command distributed forces, fight with uncrewed systems, and make decisions under pressure.

Third, we must act with urgency.

The generation that won the Battle of the Atlantic did so because they learned faster than the enemy.

We are seeing Ukraine do this right now on the front line – and we must do the same.

Perhaps most importantly of all, we must reconnect with the public.

The Battle of the Atlantic still resonates because people understood the connection between events at sea and the war writ large.

We are a maritime nation, an Island Nation – and it’s time we remembered it.

We should make that case with confidence, because many of the qualities that made Britain a maritime power remain.

London is still the global hub of maritime services, insurance, law and finance.

British expertise still shapes the rules and contracts on which global trade depends.

And our ports, shipyards and maritime businesses remain part of an ecosystem that few countries can match.

From the frigates being built on the Clyde and at Rosyth…

To the new Dreadnought submarines at Barrow…

The fleet support at Birkenhead…

Marine engineering at Tyne and Wear and advanced manufacturing in Cumbria…

Investment in the maritime is helping fuel our northern powerhouse.

Across the country, we have a thriving maritime sector worth £224 billion to the UK economy.

It supports 1.7 million jobs and 8,000 businesses….

And that’s before you consider the untapped potential.

That is why we must also reject any idea that the only future for the Royal Navy is one of decline.

Of course, the United States and China operate at a scale others cannot match.

But that does not mean Britain should lower its sights.

We can still be the greatest naval power in Europe, and one of the world’s most powerful navies.

We should not forget just how important our capabilities are, nor the influence and credibility that gives us among our allies.

From aircraft carriers to F35s…

To SSBNs and SSNs…

From frigates and destroyers to the Royal Marines.

Through the Hybrid Navy, we also have a chance to lead the global maritime autonomy race, creating military advantage while generating new economic growth.

We must match this with a serious shipbuilding strategy: ships built in Britain, for us, and exported from Britain, for our allies.

That must surely be the vision: a stronger Navy, a stronger economy, and a stronger maritime nation.

The Battle of the Atlantic was a battle for survival.

It proved that Britain’s ability to determine its own future depended on our naval power, on our ability to remain connected to the wider world.

That lesson endures.

The threat has evolved, the High North has regained strategic prominence, and the seabed has become contested.

New vulnerabilities have emerged, and so have new opportunities.

But one truth remains constant: we depend on the sea.

The Royal Navy’s task is to ensure that, with our allies, with industry, and with the whole maritime nation behind us, Britain is ready.

Ready to lead. Ready to fight. Ready to win.

The Battle of the Atlantic is one of the most important chapters in our history.

And when our own history is written, I am certain the Atlantic will prove decisive once again.

Thank you.

items.title: AI military targeting may move faster than humans can authenticate, critics warn
items.author: Natalie Oliverio
items.summary: AI military targeting may move faster than humans can authenticate, critics warned during a Wednesday hearing in Washington.
items.body:
A U.S. Navy guided-missile destroyer fires a Tomahawk missile in support of Operation Epic Fury, Feb. 28, 2026. (U.S. Navy)

Human approval may not be enough to ensure manual control over AI-enabled decisions , witnesses told Congress Wednesday, as artificial intelligence takes on a greater role in military target identification and recommendations, and in turn, compresses time available to intervene.

The concern, critics say, is not limited to weapons that can select and engage targets on their own.

At the hearing, titled “Artificial Intelligence in the Military Domain: Implications for Human Rights,” witnesses told members of the Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission that AI can influence human decisions leading to a strike while leaving the individual formally responsible for the final call.

“The approval button alone does not demonstrate the control,” Anna Mysyshyn, a Ukrainian AI-governance researcher, told lawmakers.

The issue comes as the Pentagon pushes to use AI to accelerate military decision-making. The Pentagon’s 2023 AI adoption strategy identified “fast, precise and resilient kill chains” as a desired outcome, while its 2026 AI strategy calls for becoming an “AI-first” warfighting force by redesigning military workflows and operational concepts around current AI capabilities.

Mysyshyn questioned whether a person supervising multiple AI-enabled systems can recognize an incorrect recommendation and intervene fast enough before harm occurs. She cited Ukraine as an example of AI compressing decisions from hours to minutes.

In many scenarios, a human making the final decision does not necessarily have enough information, time or the ability to challenge the system’s recommendation, she said.

The Defense Department’s 2023 directive on autonomy in weapon systems requires autonomous and semi-autonomous weapons to allow commanders and operators to exercise appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force.

Wednesday’s testimony focused on a broader question: whether that judgment remains meaningful if AI is influencing targeting faster than a human can authenticate.

Amanda Klasing, national director of government relations and advocacy at Amnesty International USA, warned that AI can compress the military “kill chain” in ways that make it difficult to determine whether meaningful human discernment actually occurred before a strike.

Joseph Chapa, a former military officer and scholar of military ethics, argued that the debate should not focus solely on how autonomous a system is. He urged policymakers to consider whether an AI system relies on statistical inference, what happens when it fails in a particular operational environment and whether its decisions can be audited afterward.

Statistical AI systems can fail differently from traditional software, Chapa said, including producing substantially different outputs from relatively small changes in inputs. More complex systems can also make it difficult to reconstruct how a particular recommendation was produced after the fact.

He called for greater AI education across the military, including specialized training for personnel working with targeting and intelligence systems.

Witnesses on Wednesday also pointed to a larger accountability problem: determining what happens when an AI-assisted decision results in civilian harm.

The Defense Department established its Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response Action Plan in 2022, including a Civilian Protection Center of Excellence intended to serve as a hub for analysis and training. Federal law requires the Pentagon to operate the center.

But a Defense Department inspector general review released in May assessed the department’s implementation of the civilian-harm framework and found problems including the loss or reassignment of personnel, the end of funding for a civilian-harm data-management platform and the failure of a senior steering committee to continue meeting.

That matters in the case of AI because, as Klasing noted, the military currently has limited ability to determine whether AI may contribute to improper targeting of civilians.

On the first day of the U.S.-Iran war, a Tomahawk cruise missile struck Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab, southern Iran. At least 168 people were killed — more than 100 of them under the age of 12, according to UN and Iranian officials.

The school building sat fewer than 100 yards from a long-time Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval installation and was previously located within the IRGC compound perimeter until a wall appeared between 2013 and 2016, according to an analysis of satellite imagery by Amnesty International .

By the time the U.S. and Israel launched their first strikes on Feb. 28, the school had been established several years prior. It was active on social media and had its own website, a Reuters investigation found.

More than 120 House Democrats sent a letter to the Pentagon on March 12 , demanding clarity on whether artificial intelligence, “including the use of the Maven Smart System, [was] used to identify the Shajareh Tayyebeh school as a target.”

U.S. military investigators in the wake of the incident stated that the strike was likely carried out by U.S. forces. The Pentagon, however, has still not released its investigative findings.

Klasing proposed adding information about AI involvement to the Pentagon’s annual civilian-casualty reports required under Section 1057 of the National Defense Authorization Act. The existing reporting requirement calls for information about civilian casualty mitigation efforts and investigations, but does not specifically require the department to identify whether AI contributed to an incident.

Steve Feldstein, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said the Pentagon should collect data from military operations and conduct after-action reviews to determine whether AI-assisted systems accurately identified intended targets and whether errors contributed to civilian casualties.

“A bigger question is to what extent is the Pentagon collecting data and verifying the target accuracy of all these 1000s of strikes?” Feldstein said.

Feldstein also cautioned against treating AI itself as the source of every potential problem. AI can be used to help verify intelligence, detect changes in imagery and prioritize defensive responses to threats such as drones and ballistic missiles.

But if a human-influenced system is built around assumptions that certain demographic traits make someone a lawful target, Mysyshyn said, AI would not correct that underlying premise.

Feldstein similarly pointed to the rules humans establish before an AI system is used. If commanders determine that a particular level of civilian harm is acceptable in pursuit of a military objective, he said, the machine is operating within a human-defined framework.

The challenge is particularly acute when systems operate faster than people can meaningfully assess recommendations.

The commission opened Wednesday’s hearing with an example from Iraq. In 2004, Army squad leader Nick Ellison encountered two young men firing a machine gun from a car during a census patrol in Kirkuk.

Ellison made eye contact with one of the men, saw panic and ordered his soldiers to hold fire. The men turned out to be brothers of a newly married groom, and the gunfire was celebratory.

Mysyshyn said testing should examine bias, reliability, civilian protection, realistic time pressure, whether operators can interrupt systems and whether decisions can be traced throughout an AI system’s lifecycle.

Chapa said some AI systems may be difficult to audit after the fact, while Deborah Brown of Human Rights Watch said information about military AI use has often emerged through investigative reporting and whistleblowers rather than government disclosures.

The growing challenge, according to witnesses, is no longer making a machine pull a trigger, but whether the human who approves the trigger pull has enough time, information and authority to make a meaningful choice before disaster.

Military Times reporter Katie Livingstone contributed to this report.

Natalie Oliverio is an independent journalist and Navy veteran who covers military and veterans’ issues. Drawing on her experience as a talent executive and mentor, she writes about the policies, people and programs shaping the military community.

items.title: How the Space Force Is Preparing for Its New Moving Target Missions
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: As the Space Force prepares to field new fleets of satellites that can track moving targets in the air and on the ground, it’s working to ensure it has the organizational structures in place to onboard and operate those systems. The post How the Space Force Is Preparing for Its New Moving Target Missions appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —As the Space Force prepares to field new fleets of satellites that can track moving targets in the air and on the ground, it’s working to ensure it has the organizational structures in place to onboard and operate those systems.

The U.S. military has long relied on large aircraft like the E-3 Sentry to track airborne targets, but leaders have become increasingly concerned that those platforms are vulnerable to long-range weapons. In recent years, the Space Force and the National Reconnaissance Office have been working to leverage satellites for the mission, an approach leaders expect will make the capability more resilient against adversaries’ anti-access/aerial-denial systems.

While the effort is still nascent and there’s much to prove about the ability of a satellite constellation to provide timely, clear tracks of moving targets like drones, missiles, and aircraft, the Pentagon has made some strides to demonstrate viability.

The NRO has launched some ground moving target indicator, or GMTI, satellites as part of its multimission proliferated low-Earth orbit constellation . And the head of Combat Forces Command, Lt. Gen. Gregory Gagnon, told reporters Sept. 16 that the Space Force expects to launch a new GMTI capability called Resilient Radar System-Ground in the next year or two. Those spacecraft are being built by Northrop Grumman, he said during a briefing at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.

The Space Force is also on the verge of launching its first space-based air moving target indicator, or AMTI , satellites. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 the spacecraft would launch later this month. Acquisition officials have declined to detail how many satellites will launch or provide a date for the mission. The only Space Force launch scheduled for this month, according to Spaceflight Now’s public launch listing , is USSF-259, a classified payload slated to lift off Sept. 16 from Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.

The service awarded SpaceX a contract in May worth up to $4.2 billion to begin building out the AMTI constellation. The company is one of 12 vendors selected to compete for space-based AMTI contracts.

Col. Ryan Frazier, the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for space-based sensing and targeting, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in July the service expects to have a “usable” space-based AMTI capability by 2028 , noting that those satellites will be a first step toward an on-orbit targeting capability but not a full solution.

“Is it everything the joint force requires? I think that will probably extend beyond ‘28,” Frazier said. “But we are going to have capabilities they don’t have today. … We’ll be able to do things that are high-value or value-added. We won’t be able to do them everywhere all the time.”

Frazier told reporters Sept. 15 that the first space-based AMTI deliveries will provide a baseline for the rest of the architecture, allowing the Space Force to fine-tune and calibrate its satellites and processing algorithms.

“There’s a broader architecture that we need to build out for the joint force to be able to close on its long-range kill chain missions,” he said. “There’s how you battle manage with that data, how you apply the processing algorithms, get that data to the weapons and the shooters that you need, and the time latencies that requires.”

As the acquisition community develops and demonstrates new systems to perform the mission, the Space Force is standing up the operational units that will manage them. On July 31, CFC activated the 77th Surveillance Squadron within Space Delta 7. The role of the 77th is to take the intelligence collected by those AMTI and GMTI satellites and deliver it to decision-makers who will determine whether to attack a particular target.

“They will use information provided from the space layer, fuse that with other sources of information and intelligence, and make decisions about weapons engagement,” Gagnon said.

Meanwhile, U.S. Space Command is working with other combatant commands and the intelligence community to craft a concept of operations for the new mission area—a document that will describe how military operators will put the system to use. SPACECOM Commander Gen. Stephen Whiting told reporters Sept. 16 his team is working with the Space Force and the NRO to solidify a plan to transition those satellites to the command once they’re deemed ready for operations.

“This will be new and different as we elevate AMTI and GMTI to space,” Whiting said. “But we do have decades of lessons learned from AMTI and GMTI in other domains.”

items.title: Lockheed’s New Modular JASSM Offers Swappable Noses and Launch Options
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: Lockheed Martin has unveiled its concept for a modular version of one of the Air Force’s main air-to-ground cruise missiles, opening up a range of possible upgrades and uses for the weapon. The post Lockheed’s New Modular JASSM Offers Swappable Noses and Launch Options appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —Lockheed Martin has unveiled its concept for a modular version of one of the Air Force’s main air-to-ground cruise missiles, opening up a range of possible upgrades and uses for the weapon.

Lockheed revealed the AGM-158 FLEX airframe, based on the Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile, at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week. The airframe has a removable nose cone to let users swap in different sensors and a reconfigurable tail for different launch options.

“The AGM-158 FLEX airframe concept was driven by a strategic need to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats, insert emerging technologies quickly, manage obsolescence, and provide, at scale, a cost-effective missile family that can be repurposed for a wide range of missions while delivering timely, relevant capability to the warfighter,” a Lockheed Martin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine via email.

The spokesperson did not answer questions about whether the Air Force has contracted or ordered the FLEX or what stage of development the project is in. Lockheed did say in a release that it has invested $35 million of its own money on the idea, based on what the firm called “a demand from our customers to have increased options.”

The Air Force has shown interest in modular munitions before—in January 2025, the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center published a notice to industry seeking technology to allow for its Extended Range Attack Munition project to have modular parts for its subcomponents. The ERAM is also a standoff cruise missile, which the Air Force rercently developed as a low-cost option to bolster its stockpiles.

Indeed, the Air Force and the rest of the U.S. military are keen to build up their weapons stocks after using thousands to strike Iran during the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The U.S. used 1,100 JASSMs over just the first 39 days of the conflict, according to an analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies in April.

Given that high usage and demand, the Air Force plans to significantly ramp up production of JASSM and its Long-Range Anti-Ship variant—and Lockheed sees FLEX as a way to further bolster the stockpile with more options.

The concept “will allow customers to quickly integrate capabilities,” Lockheed’s release states, and allow JASSM to be configured for surface, sub-surface, and ground launch options.

The air-launched version will remain compatible with all current and future JASSM and LRASM air-launched platforms.

Size options include a 206-inch extreme range option, the same size as the existing JASSM-XR, and a 168-inch extended range version, the same size as the JASSM-ER.

Both are built to give users “significantly increased standoff attack range.”

The weapon could feature in the latest iteration of a yearslong effort known as “Rapid Dragon,” which has now shifted to become “Dragon Cart,” a project to launch cruise missiles from palletized loads dropped from the ramps of transport and cargo aircraft such as the C-130 and C-17.

“As Rapid Dragon transitions into a Dragon Cart program of record, it becomes a viable deployment platform for a variety of Air Force munitions, both in inventory and in development,” the Lockheed spokesperson wrote. “While we can’t offer specific examples today, Lockheed Martin does consider all potential launch platforms in maturing munition offerings.”

items.title: The Only Air Force Fighter Pilot in Congress Wants ‘Wingmen to Come Join Me’
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: When the 119th Congress took office in January 2025, it counted a record seven former Navy SEALs among its members—and just one former Air Force fighter pilot. Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), a former F-15 and F-22 pilot, says that must change to help the Air Force get the resources it needs to recapitalize. The post The Only Air Force Fighter Pilot in Congress Wants ‘Wingmen to Come Join Me’ appeared first on Air &
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —When the 119th Congress took office in January 2025, it counted a record seven former Navy SEALs among its members—and just one former Air Force fighter pilot.

Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), an Air Force veteran who flew F-15 and F-22 fighters, says that needs to change so the Air Force gets the resources it needs to recapitalize its rapidly aging air fleet.

“I am the only fifth-generation pilot in Congress,” Pfluger said Sept. 16 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. “I need some wingmen to come join me. … God bless my Navy SEAL friends, and they are dear friends, but we’ve got a lot of them in Congress. What we don’t have is a lot of air and space expertise.”

Indeed, among the 96 veterans now in Congress, just 15 are Air Force veterans: only 15.6 percent. By comparison, there are 45 Army vets, 24 Navy vets, and 12 former Marines. The Space Force isn’t seven years old yet, but no former Space Force Guardians have been elected to Congress.

Of the 15 former Airmen on Capitol Hill, Pfluger is not the only aviator—Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) flew on the EC-130H and RC-135, Rep. Troy Downing (R-Mont.) was in combat search and rescue, and Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa) was an airborne intelligence officer.

But there are no other USAF fighter pilots. In 2022, Pfluger started the “Mach 1” caucus with three former Navy fighter pilots. Four years and two elections later, the Mach 1 caucus has gone from four to three members: Pfluger, Rep. Jake Ellzey (R-Texas), and Rep. Scott Franklin (R-Fla.).

With such small numbers, Pfluger said, it’s harder for the Air Force to “tell its story.”

“What I have done in Congress is try to educate my colleagues on what the Department of the Air Force does and why we, as a department, are really carrying the load in each of the conflicts—whether it’s Epic Fury, Midnight Hammer, Absolute Resolve, or any of the previous conflicts, the Department of the Air Force has been there every single time,” Pfluger said.

Airpower, Pfluger said, is uniquely capable of providing strategic effects. But modernization—and the resources that go along with it—is desperately needed.

We … need the help to make the case that while we are the oldest and the smallest, it’s not too late. We can recapitalize,” Pfluger said, lamenting that budget increases cannot be split evenly among the services if the Air Force is to shoulder much of the operational load.

More Airmen in Congress would help him make the case to other lawmakers, Pfluger said. For now, he gets help from Representatives and Senators who represent key Air Force installations. But he also urged Air Force leaders to make their case to Congress.

“We need Air Force leaders to be bold,” Pfluger said. “We need you to be bold to tell the truth, to say we’re underfunded.”

Multiyear Procurement

While the Air Force needs to make its case to Congress, Congress can help the Air Force by not only providing more resources, but making those resources more consistent.

Pentagon officials frequently decry the effects of continuing resolutions and government shutdowns when lawmakers fail to pass appropriations on time.

A more “predictable environment” is important, Pfluger agreed. One way to do that is multiyear procurement authorities—letting the Pentagon award contracts for multiple years instead of being reliant on annual cycles. Congress must approve any and all programs for which Pentagon wants to use multiyear procurement.

Defense officials say multiyear procurement saves the government money by locking in lower prices and helps industry by providing a stable demand signal. In the past, lawmakers have raised concerns about oversight, but they have grown increasingly open to granting more authorities.

Congress has already implemented multiyear procurement for a range of munitions programs, but members of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees have voted to authorize it for the F-35 and F-15EX as part of the 2027 defense policy bill. That bill is still pending, but Pfluger projected confidence that expanded multiyear procurement authorities are coming.

“I’m very convinced that we’re very close to getting some of these things accomplished,” Pfluger said

items.title: Air Force Eyes New-Build F-16s to Boost Fighter Force
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: The Air Force will consider acquiring new F-16 Fighting Falcon jets to answer capacity shortfalls in its aging fighter fleet, according to multiple people familiar with the matter. These discussions are happening as the Air Force is building its proposed fiscal 2028 budget and the five-year spending plan that goes with it. The post Air Force Eyes New-Build F-16s to Boost Fighter Force appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .<
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Air Force will consider acquiring new F-16 Fighting Falcon jets to help fill capacity shortfalls in its aging fighter fleet, multiple people familiar with the matter told Air & Space Forces Magazine. These discussions are happening as the Air Force is building its proposed fiscal 2028 budget and the five-year spending plan that goes with it.

Buying new F-16s—which would be the U.S.’s first in more than 20 years—is viewed as one way to quickly build back lost fighter capacity, as Lockheed Martin continues to operate a hot production line for the aircraft. Buying F-16s from Lockheed, which also produces the F-35 Lightning II, would have parallels to the decision to acquire F-15EX Eagle IIs from Boeing, which likewise came after a yearslong gap in USAF purchases.

The new-build F-16s, potentially dubbed “F-16G” to reflect upgrades from existing F-16C and D models, could be on the agenda for discussion when Air Force four-stars gather this fall for a Corona gathering of top service officials.

Lockheed Martin deferred questions to the Air Force: “This topic is best addressed by the U.S. government, but we stand ready to support the U.S. Air Force and its mission needs,” Lockheed said in a statement. “Our proven products are the backbone of the USAF fleet and provide the most advanced and versatile capabilities to ensure air dominance now and decades to come.”

The Air Force, in a written response to Air & Space Forces Magazine, said it is examining its options as it looks to the future.

“The Department of the Air Force is in initial phases of analyzing options for the next Future Years Defense Program,” an Air Force spokesperson said. “At this stage, we have neither defined the precise mission requirements nor the spectrum of options that could fill it.”

Lockheed currently produces F-16E and F models, single- and dual-seat variants respectively, for the United Arab Emirates. The company moved its production line for Block 70 F-16s in 2019 from Fort Worth, Texas, to Greenville, S.C.

If the Air Force decided to buy more F-16s, Lockheed would likely keep its Greenville production line going. The potential upgraded F-16 from that line is being referred to as a G model by those familiar with the discussions.

Inside Defense reported in December 2025 the Air Force had made inquiries with Lockheed about the pricing for new F-16s.

The Air Force today has 826 F-16s in its inventory, with 484 of those operated by the Active-Duty force. The jets average 34 years old, however, and the newest in the inventory have been flying since 2005.

USAF F-16s carry out a variety of critical missions, including air-to-air and air-to-ground strikes. F-16s that carry out suppression of enemy air defense missions are referred to as “Wild Weasels” and have seen heavy action in operations against Iran.

New F-16 purchases would drive other movement in the industry. Both Pratt & Whitney and GE Aerospace make engines that go on the F-16. Pratt, which is owned by RTX, announced Sept. 15 it has licensed Hermeus to manufacture its F100-PW-229 used on the F-15 and F-16, saying the agreement will strengthen the U.S. defense industrial base by creating a new source for the widely used engine.

Northrop Grumman, which is developing two major upgrades for existing F-16s, would also likely benefit. The company is working on the Integrated Viper Electronic Warfare Suite, or IVEWS, and an upgraded large aperture targeting pod called LITENING LA.

IVEWS, also known as the AN/ALQ-257, is an advanced electronic warfare system providing radar warning, active jamming, and detecting, identifying and locating of potential threats.

Inside Defense reported in December 2025 that the Air Force was exploring options for possibly buying new F-16s.

A source familiar with the issue, who asked not to be named to speak more freely, said any new F-16 would likely have IVEWS and multiple other new capabilities placing it not only beyond the legacy C and D fighters, but also the Block 70 fighters Lockheed is currently building.

“If the Air Force were to buy a new F-16, this would not be your grandfather’s F-16,” the source said. “This would be more akin to buying an F-15EX.”

The source said buying more F-16s would make sense for the Air Force, since Lockheed and Boeing are facing capacity constraints limiting how many F-35As and F-15EXs, respectively, they can build. And the service’s existing fleet of F-16s has been flown hard in the wars of recent decades, the source said.

“There’s only so many times you can do a service life extension program before you begin to lose the strength and integrity of the airframe itself,” the source said.

The Air Force’s new Collaborative Combat Aircraft will take part in their first large-force engagement exercise in December, the head of the drones’ Experimental Operations Unit said Sept. 15.

items.title: US ‘not prepared’ to respond to nuclear attacks in space, report says
items.author: Katie Livingstone
items.summary: A recent war-gaming report found that the U.S. has no tested response to a nuclear detonation in space.
items.body:
Air Warfare

US ‘not prepared’ to respond to nuclear attacks in space, report says

An evening launch of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, April 1, 2024. (Mike Blake/Reuters)

KYIV, Ukraine — The possibility of an adversary detonating a nuclear weapon in space to disrupt U.S. satellite infrastructure and the global communications networks that rely on it is no longer a remote scenario, according to multiple officials — and American forces are not prepared for it, strategists found after bringing former officials together to war-game their responses to a potential nuclear danger in orbit.

The possibility of nuclear war in space mostly sat in think-tank territory until recently, when the Pentagon confirmed it keeps weapons above the sky. Moscow demanded the demilitarization of space and Ukrainian intelligence published stolen documents on Russia’s next-generation military space platform all within the span of a few weeks.

But U.S. decision-makers still lack clear guidance, legal clarity and operational plans for a space-based nuclear crisis, according to an April 2026 report published by the American Foreign Policy Council that analyzed the outcome of a pair of 2025 war games that tested possible responses to such a crisis. The report found the U.S. unprepared in each case.

The war games were conducted during two workshops in May 2025 with former officials from the National Security Council, the Pentagon, the intelligence community, the Space Force, U.S. Space Command and the commercial satellite industry, using three draft contingency plans: one for a suspected nuclear device in orbit; a confirmed weapon used for coercion; and a detonation.

The plans were applied to four scenarios using a fictional Russian satellite modeled on a real Russian platform along with a Chinese adversary as stand-ins.

The first found U.S. detection and attribution tools too weak to confirm a suspected payload, with a high risk of premature escalation.

In the second scenario, Russia announced it had a nuclear weapon in orbit and warned the U.S. that it must comply with its demands or lose its military and commercial satellites — a threat the workshop judged credible and one against which the U.S. “appears to lack response options.”

The third and fourth detonated a weapon outright, first in low orbit and then in geostationary orbit as a Chinese demonstration during a Taiwan crisis, with strategists finding no capability in existence to recover from either.

Across all four scenarios, the report concluded that the U.S. can defend its own satellites against an adversary’s direct action, but it has no tested plan for detecting, managing or recovering from an adversary’s nuclear weapon in orbit.

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink confirmed on Monday that the United States “now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action,” the first public acknowledgment by any American official that the U.S. military has put weapons in orbit.

Although U.S. officials have said there was a “serious national security threat” tied to Russian space activity, including a nuclear-capable anti-satellite weapon since mid-2024, Meink’s confirmation this week prompted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov to declare on Tuesday that “We believe that space must be free of any weapon,” according to AFP .

And last week, Ukrainian military intelligence said it breached the network of Russia’s Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology, the corporation behind the Yars and Bulava nuclear missiles, and came away with documents on a Russian orbital program — including “a scalable, unified space platform called ‘Tiporyad,’ aimed at enhancing the reconnaissance, communication, and command capabilities of the Russian army,” the directorate said .

U.S. Space Command said in April it was aware of Russia’s recent orbital upgrades and the dangers they pose to American interests.

“Russia remains a very historic and sophisticated space power... they continue to invest in counter-space weapons, with the most concerning reports being that they are potentially thinking about placing on orbit a nuclear ASAT weapon,” Gen. Stephen Whiting, head of U.S. Space Command, told Fox News on April 16.

Such a weapon “would hold at risk everyone’s satellites in low Earth orbit, and that would be an outcome that we just couldn’t tolerate,” he said.

Katie Livingstone is the Ukraine correspondent for Defense News and Military Times. Based in Kyiv, she has covered Russia's full-scale invasion since its first days. She is a former Fulbright fellow whose award-winning work has appeared in outlets across Europe and the U.S.

items.title: Israel’s SPICE 1000 bombs can soon drop from F-35 fighters
items.author: Tzally Greenberg
items.summary: The Israeli air force can look forward to yet another bomb type for its F-35 fleet.
items.body:
Mideast Africa

Israel’s SPICE 1000 bombs can soon drop from F-35 fighters

An Israeli F-35I Adir taxis out for a drill during Red Flag at Nellis Air Force Base, Nev., on March, 15 2023. (William R. Lewis/U.S. Air Force)

JERUSALEM — Israel’s SPICE 1000 bomb technology will soon be droppable from the country’s F-35 fighter aircraft, manufacturer Rafael Advanced Defense Systems announced on Wednesday.

The Israeli company states that the integration work is being executed as a joint initiative between Rafael and Lockheed Martin, the aircraft’s manufacturer, at Lockheed’s facilities in the United States. Development and testing are expected to conclude within a few months, according to the firm.

Following completion, the munition will be formally cleared for operational employment by the Israeli Air Force’s F-35 fleet. At a later stage, the capability is set to become available to F-35 operators worldwide.

The SPICE 1000 technology converts general-purpose and penetration warheads of 1,000 lbs into precision-capable munitions that pilots can drop from 75 miles away thanks to gliding wings on the bomb’s body. It is part of the company’s SPICE family that includes additional weight classes: the SPICE 2000 and the SPICE 250.

Rafael notes that SPICE 1000 bombs have served as a primary munition of the Israeli Air Force on F-15s and F-16s for several years, including in the recent war against Iran.

Rafael said it has sold the SPICE 1000 to several countries, but didn’t specify which. One customer emerged in December 2025 when India’s Defense Acquisition Council (DAC) approved the procurement of SPICE 1000 systems.

The Israeli Air Force maintains an active fleet of approximately fifty F-35I (“Adir”) aircrafts, and upon completion of all approved procurement processes, including the purchase of 25 aircraft this past May, Israel is projected to hold a fleet of 100 stealth fighters in total.

Tzally Greenberg is the Israel correspondent for Defense News. He has experience reporting on economic affairs as well as defense and cyber companies.

items.title: Ministry of Defence confirms the death of Major Paul Wilks
items.summary: It is with great sadness that the Ministry of Defence must confirm the death of Major Paul Wilks, who died in Ukraine on 12 September 2026.
items.body:
Major Paul Wilks died in a tragic road traffic incident, away from the front lines. He was 40 years old.

Major Wilks was born on 13 November 1985. He commissioned from Sandhurst on 14 April 2012 joining the Intelligence Corps where he remained throughout his career, successfully promoting to the rank of Major. Major Wilks had deployed on multiple operational tours including to Afghanistan. He was recognised for this service with two Operational Service Medals. He was also recently awarded the Long Service and Good Conduct Medal on 7 May 2026.

Major Wilks was an exceptionally bright and professional officer who embodied the best of the UK military. He was a gifted leader who earned the admiration and respect of all those fortunate enough to have served alongside him. He was a formidable officer, colleague and friend to all those who knew him.

Above all, Major Wilks was a proud family man and was devoted to his wife and two sons.

His Commanding Officer said:

It is with profound sadness that we honour the memory of Major Paul Wilks. Even in high-pressure environments, Paul maintained a sharp sense of humour and a genuine warmth that connected him to everyone in this unit. He was a man of great intellect, yet he remained a mate to those he served with. He spoke often of his love for his wife and two sons, expressing his deep gratitude for the support they provided, which allowed him to serve with such distinction. It is because of that foundation that he was able to meet the challenges of his role, and it is in the course of his devotion to duty that he made the ultimate sacrifice. Major Wilks represented the finest traditions of UK Defence. It was a privilege to serve alongside him. We will miss him.

items.title: US military must adapt as formations will be ‘hunted’ by autonomous systems, Caine says
items.author: Cristina Stassis
items.summary: Technology, such as AI and autonomous systems, is changing the character of war, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine said.
items.body:
MilTech

US military must adapt as formations will be ‘hunted’ by autonomous systems, Caine says

Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine attend a House Appropriations Subcommittee on the FY2027 budget request for the DoD. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)

Gen. Dan Caine , chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, emphasized that the joint force must prove readiness ahead of a conflict in a time when adversaries are becoming increasingly interconnected amid the changing character of war .

The force needs to be “clear-eyed” about the environment ahead as future conflicts will be progressively contested and defy simpler solutions, Caine said in a Wednesday keynote at the Air & Space Forces Association’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference .

“We have to assume from now on that our formations will be hunted by autonomous systems, jammed across the spectrum and tracked in real time,” Caine said in his speech.

“We have to transition the joint force to be prepared to fight and win our future wars by generating and delivering lethality at scale with an agile, optimized, high-low mix of combat capabilities to give the young members of the 2.8 million-member all-volunteer joint force the tools that they need before they need them,” he continued.

While calling the American military and their families the country’s “ultimate insurance policy,” Caine asserted that the joint force needs to be ready for a fight before it begins.

Even as the country’s adversaries are geographically dispersed, they are connected through sharing technology, intelligence, weapons and economic support, he said. As the military branches study past and present American battlefields, they are looking for new ways to challenge the advantage, demonstrating the necessity for readiness and investment in a range of military capabilities before a crisis begins.

Recently, Russia and Iran have deepened their military partnership with a technological feedback loop amid the Ukraine war and the conflict in the Middle East. Moscow is sending Iran upgraded munitions, satellite imagery and targeting data that have been used against American forces in the Middle East.

Tehran first supplied Russia with Shahed attack drones for use in Ukraine in 2022 and has since arranged a license to build the Iranian-designed drones on Russian territory.

“The character of war is changing, and time is of the essence,” Caine said, emphasizing how the way and speed in which countries fight is altering on the modern battlefield as artificial intelligence, cyber capabilities and autonomous systems develop.

The chairman noted that the modern battlefield today operates from the seabed to the cislunar space, highlighting that the advantage will go to whoever can see, understand, decide and act first as a learning organization.

Caine highlighted the June rescue of two Army soldiers by way of a remotely piloted Navy unmanned surface as an example of how the military is adapting and utilizing AI and autonomous tools.

He also referenced how these tools are being used to change the threat in contested electromagnetic interference environments, such as in Ukraine, with first-person view drones.

“Take it together, these examples from the Strait of Hormuz to the front lines in Ukraine show how quickly technology is changing the character of war,” he said.

Caine spotlighted that it will be young service leaders who will be the ones in charge of the subsequent conflicts in these environments and will have to be adaptive and understanding of their environment with a plethora of information.

As technology, networks and software continue to change, the need for capable and lethal leaders will not, he said. The nation can bring autonomy and better networks to the force but none of it will matter without trusted leaders that can work under pressure.

“We must move together because the window to build the force that we need is closing,” Caine said. “We can buy almost anything in life, but we cannot buy time.”

Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.
